SYNCOPE ASSESSMENT
==================

PC: Episode of collapse / transient loss of consciousness

HPC:

Duration LOC: _________ seconds/minutes
Position:     standing / sitting / lying

PRODROME (ask carefully):
□ Lightheadedness / presyncope      □ Palpitations
□ Chest pain / chest tightness      □ Shortness of breath
□ Nausea / diaphoresis              □ Visual disturbance
□ None (sudden onset)               □ Aura ___________

WITNESSED (if yes):
□ Pallor     □ Cyanosis     □ Tonic-clonic movements
□ Eye deviation   □ Incontinence   □ Tongue biting
Duration of abnormal movements: _________

POST-EVENT:
Recovery to baseline:  immediate / ___ minutes
Post-ictal confusion:  Y / N
Headache after:        Y / N
Weakness after:        Y / N

PREVIOUS EPISODES:  Y / N    How many: _____   First ever: Y / N

CARDIAC RED FLAGS (ask specifically):
□ Exercise-induced syncope
□ No prodrome / sudden onset
□ Syncope lying down
□ Palpitations immediately before
□ Family history SCD / arrhythmia / cardiomyopathy (<40 yrs)
□ Known structural heart disease / congenital heart disease
□ Chest pain associated

ORTHOSTATIC SYMPTOMS:
□ Worse on standing       □ Recent fluid loss / dehydration
□ Recent medication change (antihypertensives, diuretics)

MEDICATIONS: _________________________________
(Antihypertensives / beta-blockers / QT-prolonging drugs / diuretics / nitrates)

PMHx: □ IHD   □ AF   □ HF   □ Epilepsy   □ Diabetes   □ Hypertension
FHx SCD: Y / N — detail: ____________________
Social: EtOH ___   Drugs ___

EXAMINATION:
Vitals: HR ___ (reg/irreg)   BP ___/___   Lying BP ___/___   Standing BP ___/___
SpO2 ____%   RR ___   Temp ___
Heart sounds: normal / murmur: ____________
Neuro: GCS ___/15   Focal deficit: Y / N
Skin: pale / clammy / flushed

ORTHOSTATIC DROP: Δ systolic ≥20mmHg or Δ diastolic ≥10mmHg on standing = positive

ECG:
Rate: ___  Rhythm: _________
PR: ___ms  QRS: ___ms  QTc: ___ms (nl <440M / <460F)
□ Normal   □ BBB (L/R)   □ Bifascicular block   □ Long QT
□ Short PR / delta wave (WPW)   □ Brugada pattern (RBBB + STE V1-3)
□ Epsilon wave / T-inv V1-4 (ARVD)   □ ST changes: _________
□ AV block (degree: ___)   □ Arrhythmia: _________

RISK STRATIFICATION (Canadian Syncope Risk Score):
□ Heart disease (known or suspected on ECG)  +4
□ Systolic BP <90 or >180 on arrival         +3
□ Troponin elevated                          +3
□ Abnormal QRS axis (<-30 or >100°)         +2
□ QRS duration >130ms                        +2
□ Abnormal ED diagnosis (not vasovagal)      +2
□ Predisposition to vasovagal syncope        -1

Total: ___   [Low risk ≤-2; Intermediate; High risk ≥0 = admit for monitoring]

IMPRESSION:
Most likely: __________________________
Risk: low / intermediate / high

PLAN:
□ Admit for monitoring
□ Discharge with GP follow-up / outpatient Cardiology referral
□ Echocardiogram   □ 24hr Holter / prolonged cardiac monitoring
□ Safety netting: return if palpitations, exertional symptoms, recurrence
⚠️ Red Flags for Cardiac Syncope (admit all): exertional, no prodrome, palpitations, FHx SCD, abnormal ECG, known structural heart disease, age >65 + comorbidities

🫀 Cardiac (Admit)

  • Ventricular arrhythmia (VT/VF)
  • Complete heart block (3°)
  • Aortic stenosis (exertional)
  • HOCM
  • Acute MI
  • PE / dissection
  • SVT / AF
  • Sick sinus syndrome
  • Brugada / Long QT / ARVD
  • WPW

⚡ Reflex / Vasovagal

  • Vasovagal (most common)
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Situational (micturition, cough, defaecation)
  • Carotid sinus hypersensitivity
  • Post-prandial

💊 Medications / Metabolic

  • Antihypertensives — over-treatment
  • QT-prolonging drugs
  • Diuretics — volume depletion
  • Nitrates
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Anaemia

🧠 CNS Mimics

  • Seizure (ictal/post-ictal)
  • TIA / vertebrobasilar
  • Hypoxia
  • Hyperventilation
  • Anxiety / psychogenic
MANDATORY12-lead ECG
MANDATORYCapillary/venous glucose
IMPORTANThs-Troponin (0h)
IMPORTANTU&E, FBC
IMPORTANTLying & standing BP
CONSIDERD-dimer if PE risk
CONSIDERRepeat troponin (1h/3h)
CONSIDEREcho (outpatient/urgent)
CONSIDER24hr Holter
CONSIDEREEG if seizure query
1

Immediate

ABCs, lying flat, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose

2

Risk Stratify

Apply Canadian Syncope Risk Score. Admit all high-risk patients (score ≥0) for monitored bed. Intermediate risk: ED observation, repeat ECG, serial troponin.

3

Cardiogenic syncope

Urgent cardiology review. Atropine 500mcg IV for symptomatic bradycardia. Transcutaneous pacing if no response. Treat specific arrhythmia per ALS algorithm.

4

Orthostatic hypotension

IV fluids if dehydrated. Review medications. Compression stockings. Tilt training. Consider fludrocortisone via GP.

5

Vasovagal (low-risk)

Reassurance. Avoid triggers. Physical counterpressure manoeuvres. Increase fluid/salt intake. Discharge with GP follow-up. No driving until cleared.

🚗 DVLA: All syncope patients must be advised not to drive until cause established. Group 1 (car/motorcycle): notify if recurrent/unexplained. Group 2 (LGV/PSV): notify immediately. Document advice given.

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE CG109 — Transient Loss of Consciousness in Adults ↗ ESC Guidelines on Syncope (2018) ↗ Canadian Syncope Risk Score — CMAJ 2016 ↗ DVLA — Assessing Fitness to Drive

4AT DELIRIUM SCREEN:
□ Alertness (normal=0 / mild drowsiness=0 / clearly abnormal=4)
□ AMT-4 (age, DOB, place, year — each error = 1 point, max 2)
  Age: C/I __ DOB: C/I __ Place: C/I __ Year: C/I __
□ Attention (months backwards Sept-Aug-Jul… errors: 0=0 / 1=1 / 2+=2)
□ Acute change or fluctuating course (yes=4 / no=0)
4AT Score: ___/12  [≥4 = likely delirium; 1-3 = possible; 0 = unlikely]

TARGETED HISTORY (AEIOU TIPS mnemonic):
A - Alcohol (intoxication, Wernicke's, withdrawal)
E - Epilepsy / post-ictal
I - Insulin (hypoglycaemia / DKA / HHS)
O - Oxygen (hypoxia, CO poisoning, PE)
U - Uraemia / electrolytes (Na, K, Ca)

T - Trauma (head injury, subdural)
I - Infection (meningitis, encephalitis, UTI, pneumonia, sepsis)
P - Psychiatric / Pain / Polypharmacy
S - Stroke / Structural / Shock

□ Steroids □ Antibiotics  □ TCAs  □ Digoxin  □ Lithium

Pupils: L___mm (reactive Y/N)  R___mm (reactive Y/N)  Equal: Y/N

PLAN:
□ CT head    □ LP (if meningism or CT negative)
□ Septic screen   □ Urine culture   □ Blood cultures
□ Treat underlying cause
□ Monitor closely / 1:1 nursing
□ Delirium management precautions

⚡ Structural/Vascular

  • Intracranial haemorrhage (SAH/SDH/ICH)
  • Ischaemic stroke
  • CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis)
  • CVST
  • Raised ICP (mass/hydrocephalus)
  • Seizure / post-ictal

🦠 Toxic/Metabolic

  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Wernicke's encephalopathy
  • Hypoxia / hypercapnia
  • Uraemia
  • Hepatic encephalopathy
  • Hypo/hypernatraemia
  • Hypercalcaemia
  • Thyroid crisis / myxoedema
  • DKA/HHS

💊 Toxicological

  • Opioid toxidrome
  • Benzodiazepine toxicity
  • Alcohol intoxication / withdrawal
  • CO poisoning
  • Anticholinergic toxidrome
  • Serotonin syndrome
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

🦠 Infection/Systemic

  • Septic encephalopathy
  • UTI (esp. elderly)
  • Pneumonia
  • COVID-19
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Urinary retention (pain → agitation)
MANDATORYCapillary blood glucose
MANDATORYECG
MANDATORYU&E, FBC, LFTs, CRP
MANDATORYUrine dip ± MC&S
IMPORTANTTroponin, TFTs, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺
IMPORTANTBlood cultures (if febrile)
IMPORTANTParacetamol/salicylate levels
CONSIDERCT head (if focal deficit/trauma/first episode)
CONSIDERLP (if meningism / CT normal)
CONSIDERAmmonia, drug screen
CONSIDERCXR
CONSIDERVBG (lactate, pH, pCO2)
1

Immediate — Universal Antidotes

  • Glucose 10% IV 100ml if CBG <4mmol/L (or CBG not available)
  • Thiamine 500mg IV over 30min if alcohol use disorder / malnourished / any unexplained AMS (before glucose if Wernicke's suspected)
  • Naloxone 400mcg IV/IM/IN titrate if opioid toxidrome (miosis + reduced GCS + bradypnoea)
  • Oxygen to target SpO2 94-98%
2

Treat Underlying Cause

  • Meningitis: Ceftriaxone 2g IV immediately + Dexamethasone 10mg IV (do not delay for CT/LP)
  • Sepsis: cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics (per sepsis protocol)
  • DKA/HHS: insulin + fluids (see DKA protocol)
  • Hypercalcaemia: IV fluids, bisphosphonate
  • Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose, treat precipitant, rifaximin
3

Delirium Management (non-pharmacological first)

  • Quiet, well-lit environment; reorientation; familiar faces
  • Ensure glasses/hearing aids in situ
  • Avoid restraints; 1:1 nursing if needed
  • Correct sleep-wake cycle
4

Sedation if Risk to Self/Others (last resort)

Haloperidol 0.5–2mg PO/IM (avoid in Parkinson's/DLB/alcohol withdrawal/QTc prolongation)
Lorazepam 0.5–1mg IV/IM — preferred in alcohol withdrawal, seizures, NMS
Olanzapine 5–10mg IM — avoid combining with benzodiazepines IM

⚠️ NEVER give glucose without thiamine first in suspected Wernicke's — precipitates acute Korsakoff's

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE CG103 — Delirium: Prevention, Diagnosis and Management (NG20 is Coeliac Disease — corrected reference) ↗ 4AT Rapid Assessment Test for Delirium ↗ NICE NG241 — Meningitis (Bacterial) and Meningococcal Disease

HEADACHE ASSESSMENT
====================
PC: Headache  Severity (NRS 0-10): ___/10

RED FLAG SCREENING (ask ALL — any positive = investigate):
□ THUNDERCLAP — sudden onset, maximal at/within seconds ("worst ever")
□ Exertional / Valsalva onset (cough, straining, sexual activity)
□ Fever + meningism (neck stiffness, photophobia, rash)
□ New focal neurological deficit
□ Altered consciousness / confusion
□ Worsening progressive pattern (days–weeks)
□ Worse lying flat / morning headache + vomiting (raised ICP)
□ Age >50 NEW headache / headache with scalp/jaw tenderness (GCA)
□ Known cancer / immunocompromised / HIV
□ Recent head trauma
□ New headache in pregnancy / postpartum

  □ Rhinorrhoea / lacrimation / ptosis / conjunctival injection (cluster)

Usual treatment: _____________________

PMHx: migraines / cluster HA / raised ICP / malignancy / HIV / TB
      Anticoagulation: Y / N
Medications: OCP / nitrates / analgesia overuse (>15 days/month) 
FHx: migraines: Y/N   SAH / cerebrovascular disease: Y/N
Social: EtOH / smoking

EXAMINATION:
GCS: ___/15   HR: ___  BP: ___/___  Temp: ___  SpO2: ___%
Pupils: equal/reactive Y/N
Fundi (if available): papilloedema Y/N
Cranial nerves: normal / abnormal: ______________
Neck stiffness: Y / N   Jolt accentuation: Y / N
Kernig's: Y/N   Brudzinski's: Y/N
Temporal artery tenderness / pulsatility: Y/N
Skin: rash (petechial / purpuric): Y/N

Ottawa SAH Rule (apply if non-traumatic, non-thunderclap, GCS 15):
NOT applicable if: new focal deficit, previous SAH, known brain tumour
CT indicated if ANY of:
□ Age ≥40
□ Neck pain or stiffness
□ Witnessed LOC
□ Onset with exertion
□ Thunderclap (maximal at onset)
□ Limited neck flexion on exam

IMPRESSION:
Likely diagnosis: _______________________________
Red flags present: Y / N
SAH rule: requires CT — Y / N

PLAN:
□ CT head (non-contrast)   □ LP (if CT neg, >6h from onset)
□ ESR/CRP (if GCA suspected)   □ Ophthalmology (if acute angle closure)
□ Analgesia regime (see management)
□ Discharge with safety netting / admit
⚠️ Can't-Miss: SAH, meningitis/encephalitis, CVT, subdural, hypertensive emergency, temporal arteritis, CO poisoning, acute angle closure glaucoma

🚨 Life-threatening

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (thunderclap)
  • Bacterial meningitis (fever + meningism + rash)
  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (progressive + papilloedema)
  • Hypertensive emergency (BP >180/120 + end-organ damage)
  • Temporal arteritis (>50, ESR↑, jaw claudication)
  • CO poisoning (other household members affected)

⚡ Serious

  • Intracranial mass / raised ICP
  • Epidural / subdural haematoma
  • Acute angle closure glaucoma (red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil)
  • Carotid/vertebral artery dissection (neck pain + Horner's)
  • Pre-eclampsia / eclampsia

💆 Benign Primary

  • Migraine (POUND criteria)
  • Tension-type (band-like, bilateral)
  • Cluster (unilateral, retro-orbital, autonomic features)
  • Medication overuse headache
  • Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (obese women)

🌐 Systemic

  • Viral illness / fever
  • Sinusitis
  • Cervicogenic
  • Post-LP headache
  • Anaemia / dehydration
  • Herpes zoster
ℹ️ Most benign primary headaches require no investigation if the presentation is typical and there are no red flags
IMPORTANTCT head non-contrast (red flags)
IMPORTANTBP measurement
CONSIDERLP (CT neg, >6h from onset, SAH suspected)
CONSIDERESR, CRP, FBC (if GCA/infection suspected)
CONSIDERCO level (if multiple household members)
CONSIDERMRI head/MRV (CVST suspected)
CONSIDERSlit lamp / IOP (if red eye / acute glaucoma)
CONSIDERβ-hCG (pregnancy-associated headache)
1

Benign Headache / Migraine Regimen

  • Paracetamol 1g PO
  • Ibuprofen 400-600mg PO (if not contraindicated)
  • Metoclopramide 10mg IV/PO (anti-dopaminergic — also treats nausea)
  • Prochlorperazine 12.5mg IM / 3mg buccal — alternative to metoclopramide
  • IV fluids if dehydrated
  • Dexamethasone 8-12mg IV/PO — reduces migraine recurrence at 24-48h (NNT ~5)
2

Migraine-specific

  • Sumatriptan 50-100mg PO / 6mg SC / nasal spray — if not given ergotamine
  • Dark, quiet room; rest
3

Cluster Headache

  • 100% O₂ via NRB mask 12-15L/min for 15-20 min (first-line)
  • Sumatriptan 6mg SC (most effective abortive)
  • Refer to neurology / headache clinic for prophylaxis (verapamil)
4

Suspected SAH

Urgent non-contrast CT head → LP if CT negative and >6h from onset → Neurosurgery referral if positive

5

Suspected Bacterial Meningitis

DO NOT DELAY antibiotics for LP/CT. Ceftriaxone 2g IV immediately + Dexamethasone 10mg IV

6

Temporal Arteritis (GCA)

Prednisolone 60mg PO immediately (do not wait for biopsy). Urgent ophthalmology if visual symptoms. ESR, CRP, temporal artery biopsy within 1 week.

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE CG150 — Headaches in Over 12s: Diagnosis and Management ↗ BASH — British Association for the Study of Headache Guidelines ↗ NICE NG261 — Subarachnoid Haemorrhage Caused by a Ruptured Aneurysm ↗ NICE NG120 — Giant Cell Arteritis

NICE CT Head Criteria (NG232 — Adults):
Immediate CT (within 1 hour) if ANY of:
□ GCS <13 at any point since injury
□ GCS 13-14 at 2h post-injury
□ Suspected open/depressed skull fracture
□ Signs of basal skull fracture (Battle's, panda eyes, CSF rhinorrhoea/otorrhoea, haemotympanum)
□ Seizure after injury (in non-epileptic patient)
□ Focal neurological deficit
□ Age ≥65 with amnesia OR LOC OR vomiting
□ Coagulopathy/anticoagulants with LOC, amnesia or vomiting
□ ≥1 episode of vomiting (non-anticoagulated, age <65)

CT within 8 hours if (and no immediate indication above):
□ Loss of consciousness
□ Amnesia
□ Dangerous mechanism (pedestrian vs car, ejection from vehicle, fall >1m or 5 stairs)

IMPRESSION:
CT indicated: immediate / 8h / not indicated
Suspected: concussion / skull fracture / extradural haematoma / subdural / contusion
IndicationTimingCriteria
Immediate CT headWithin 1 hourGCS <13, focal deficit, skull fracture signs, post-traumatic seizure, age ≥65 with LOC/amnesia/vomiting, coagulopathy/anticoagulants with LOC/amnesia/vomiting, GCS 13-14 at 2h
CT headWithin 8 hoursLOC or amnesia (no immediate indication present); dangerous mechanism
CT C-spineAlongside head CTGCS<13, neck pain + dangerous mechanism, focal neurology, intubated patient, other distracting injury
No CT needed—GCS 15, no amnesia/LOC, no red flags, low-energy mechanism, no high-risk features
⚠️ NEXUS / CANADIAN C-SPINE: Use to guide c-spine imaging. If alert (GCS 15), no midline tenderness, no focal deficit, no painful distracting injury, no intoxication = low risk, can clinically clear.
1

Primary Survey + C-spine

ABCs with manual in-line immobilisation until C-spine cleared. O₂. IV access × 2. Cardiac monitoring.

2

Concussion (GCS 15, normal CT)

  • 24h period cognitive rest; avoid alcohol and contact sport
  • Discharge to responsible adult with written head injury advice
  • Return if: worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, confusion, weakness, drowsiness
  • Graduated return-to-play/work protocol via GP
3

Raised ICP

  • Head of bed 30°
  • Mannitol 0.25–1g/kg IV over 15-20 min — discuss with neurosurgery
  • Or Hypertonic saline (NaCl 3%) 250ml IV
  • Controlled ventilation if intubated (target PaCO₂ 4.5-5kPa; hyperventilate to 4–4.5 only as temporising for acute herniation)
4

Anticoagulation Reversal

  • Warfarin: Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (Beriplex) 25-50 units/kg IV + Vitamin K 5-10mg IV
  • DOACs — Dabigatran: Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5g IV
  • Factor Xa inhibitors: Andexanet alfa (discuss with haematology)
5

Neurosurgical Referral

Any significant intracranial haemorrhage, deteriorating GCS, mass effect/midline shift, compound depressed skull fracture, suspected penetrating injury

🚨 STATUS EPILEPTICUS PROTOCOL (NICE NG217) — Time-Critical: call for senior help early
TimeStepTreatment
0–5 minImmediateABCs, O₂, IV access, check glucose. Correct hypoglycaemia. Assess for treatable cause.
5–10 min1st-Line BenzodiazepineIV access: Lorazepam 4mg IV — can repeat once after 10 min
No IV: Buccal midazolam 10mg OR Rectal diazepam 10–20mg
Paramedic: IM midazolam 10mg
20–40 min2nd-Line (if still seizing)Choose ONE:
• Levetiracetam (Keppra) 60mg/kg IV (max 4.5g) over 10 min — preferred
• Sodium valproate 40mg/kg IV (max 3g) over 10 min — avoid in women of childbearing age
• Phenytoin 20mg/kg IV at max 50mg/min with cardiac monitoring
40+ minRefractory StatusAnaesthetic team / ICU. Consider:
• Propofol 1–2mg/kg IV then infusion
• Thiopental 100–250mg IV
• Midazolam infusion
Intubation + ITU admission + EEG monitoring
⚠️ In alcohol withdrawal or Wernicke's — give Thiamine 500mg IV before or alongside treatment. Avoid valproate if liver disease.
+

Post-Seizure (simple, self-terminating)

  • Observe until back to baseline
  • First seizure: refer to First Seizure Clinic — do NOT start AEDs in ED without neurology input
  • Known epileptic: check AED levels, address triggers, may restart/reload AED with neurology advice
  • DVLA: inform patient — must not drive for 6 months after 1st seizure / 1 year after status epilepticus
  • No provoked cause found: admit for monitoring + neurology review

🫁 Pulmonary

  • Tension pneumothorax (tracheal deviation + absent BS)
  • Anaphylaxis (stridor + urticaria)
  • Status asthmaticus
  • Massive PE
  • Simple pneumothorax
  • Pneumonia / LRTI
  • AECOPD
  • Pleural effusion
  • Pulmonary fibrosis

🫀 Cardiac

  • Cardiac tamponade
  • STEMI / ACS

🩸 Other

  • Metabolic acidosis (DKA, lactic)
  • Sepsis
  • CO poisoning
  • Opioid/sedative toxicity (↓GCS)
  • Thyrotoxicosis
  • Anxiety / hyperventilation
  • Neuromuscular (GBS, MG, ALS)

🔑 Differentiating Features

  • Sudden onset + pleuritic = pneumothorax/PE
  • Wheeze + diurnal = asthma
  • Orthopnoea + PND + oedema = CCF
  • Fever + productive cough = pneumonia
  • Immobility + tachycardia = PE
  • Stridor + angioedema = anaphylaxis

1

Immediate — Any Dyspnoea

  • Upright position, high-flow O₂ initially, IV access, monitoring
  • Target SpO2 94-98% (88-92% if known/suspected COPD)
2

Tension Pneumothorax

Clinical diagnosis — do not wait for imaging. Immediate needle decompression: 14-16G cannula 2nd ICS MCL or 4th/5th ICS AAL. Then chest drain.

3

Anaphylaxis

Adrenaline 500mcg IM (0.5ml of 1:1000) anterolateral thigh — see Anaphylaxis protocol

4

Asthma / AECOPD

Bronchodilators + steroids — see specific protocols

5

Acute Pulmonary Oedema (SCAPE)

Sit upright, NIV (CPAP), GTN infusion, furosemide — see CHF protocol

6

PE

Anticoagulation immediately — see DVT/PE protocol. tPA for massive PE with haemodynamic compromise.

⚠️ Deadly Six (PET MAC): PE, Oesophageal rupture, Tension pneumothorax, MI, Aortic dissection, Cardiac tamponade

🚨 Life-threatening

  • STEMI / ACS (central, heavy, radiation, diaphoresis)
  • Aortic dissection (tearing, maximal onset, pulse deficit)
  • Tension pneumothorax
  • Massive PE
  • Oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave — post-vomiting)
  • Cardiac tamponade

⚡ Serious

  • NSTEMI / UA
  • Pericarditis / myocarditis
  • Aortic stenosis with angina
  • Spontaneous pneumothorax
  • Submassive PE
  • Ruptured oesophageal varices

💊 Non-urgent

  • Musculoskeletal (costochondritis, Tietze's)
  • GORD / reflux
  • Oesophageal spasm
  • Pleurisy
  • Herpes zoster (dermatomal)
  • Anxiety / panic attack
  • Anaemia

🔑 Key Differentiators

  • GTN response — partial response does NOT rule in ACS
  • Reproducible tenderness — reduces but does NOT exclude ACS
  • Pleuritic character — PE, pericarditis, pneumothorax
  • Epigastric — inferior STEMI, GORD, pancreatitis

ℹ️ HEART ≤3 + negative hs-Troponin (0h/1h) = ~0.5-1% MACE risk — safe to discharge with GP follow-up in appropriate patients. HEART ≥7 = high risk, activate cardiology pathway.

ESC 0h/1h hs-Troponin Pathway

Apply only to patients presenting >3h from symptom onset. Use local laboratory thresholds.

0h ValueΔ at 1hInterpretationAction
Below rule-out threshold<5 ng/L riseRule-outDischarge if low risk (HEART ≤3, no ongoing ischaemia)
Very high (above rule-in)AnyRule-inCardiology referral for NSTEMI management
Intermediate zone≥5 ng/L riseRule-inCardiology referral for NSTEMI management
Intermediate zone<5 ng/L riseObserveFurther sampling at 3h or 6h; consider CTCA
1

All Chest Pain — Immediate

  • IV access, monitoring, 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, pain relief
  • GTN 400mcg SL — avoid in suspected RV infarct (inferior STEMI) or SBP <90
  • Morphine 2.5-5mg IV (titrate) + antiemetic if resistant to GTN
  • Supplemental O₂ only if SpO2 <94%
2

STEMI — Activate PPCI Pathway

  • Call cardiology / PPCI team immediately (target door-to-balloon <90 min)
  • Aspirin 300mg PO (chewed)
  • Ticagrelor 180mg PO (preferred) or Prasugrel 60mg (if going to PCI, <75 yrs, >60kg, no prior stroke/TIA)
  • UFH 5000 units IV bolus or Bivalirudin per local protocol
  • Thrombolysis only if PPCI unavailable within 120 min: Tenecteplase (TNKase) weight-based dose
3

NSTEMI (Troponin rise, no STE)

  • Aspirin 300mg PO
  • Ticagrelor 180mg PO
  • Fondaparinux 2.5mg SC (unless immediate angiography planned — use UFH/bivalirudin instead)
  • Cardiology review: risk stratify with GRACE score — high risk → invasive strategy within 24h
4

Aortic Dissection

  • Urgent CT aortogram
  • Target SBP 100-120mmHg: IV Labetalol (start 20mg IV, infusion 20-160mg/h) or Esmolol
  • Type A (ascending) = emergency surgery. Type B = medical management +/- TEVAR
  • Do NOT give thrombolytics or anticoagulation
5

Low Risk / Musculoskeletal

HEART ≤3 + negative hs-cTn rule-out pathway → consider discharge with follow-up. NSAIDs/paracetamol for MSK. PPI trial for GORD.

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE NG185 — Chest Pain of Recent Onset (2021) ↗ NICE NG203 — Acute Coronary Syndromes (2020) ↗ ESC Guidelines on Acute Coronary Syndromes (2023) ↗ HEART Score — Six et al., Netherlands Heart Journal 2010

1

All Abdominal Pain

  • IV access, bloods, monitor. Do not withhold analgesia — improves examination accuracy.
  • Paracetamol 1g IV + Morphine 2.5-5mg IV titrated + antiemetic
  • NBM if surgical/procedural intervention likely
2

Ruptured AAA / Vascular Emergency

Immediate surgical review. Large-bore IV ×2. Permissive hypotension (SBP ~80-90). Blood products. Emergency theatre.

3

Appendicitis

NBM, IV fluids, analgesia, surgical review. Appendicectomy (laparoscopic). Antibiotics if perforation/abscess.

4

Cholangitis (Charcot's triad = sepsis)

Resuscitate as sepsis. Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5g IV TDS (or per local protocol). Urgent ERCP ± biliary decompression. Surgical/GI review.

5

Acute Pancreatitis

  • IV fluids (aggressive in first 24h — Hartmann's preferred)
  • Analgesia (morphine as needed)
  • NBM initially; early enteral nutrition if tolerated
  • Severity scoring: Glasgow-Imrie or BISAP (admit all modified Glasgow ≥3)
  • Antibiotics only if infected necrosis confirmed
  • ERCP if gallstone pancreatitis + cholangitis/obstruction
6

Renal Colic

  • Diclofenac 75mg IM or 100mg PR (most effective) — avoid if CKD
  • Morphine 5-10mg IV/SC if NSAIDs insufficient
  • CT KUB (non-contrast) for diagnosis
  • Urology referral if stone >6mm, infection, single kidney, or obstruction

🚨 Ectopic Until Proven Otherwise: Any reproductive-age female with pelvic pain + positive β-hCG with no confirmed IUP. Haemodynamic instability = surgical emergency → theatre immediately.
1

Ruptured Ectopic (Haemodynamically Unstable)

O⁻ blood immediately. Large-bore IV ×2. Theatre. Gynaecology emergency call. Do NOT wait for USS confirmation if unstable.

2

Stable Suspected Ectopic

  • TVUS + quantitative β-hCG
  • Gynaecology review: expectant / methotrexate / laparoscopy depending on β-hCG level and clinical picture
  • Anti-D 250IU IM if Rh-negative
3

PID / Salpingitis

  • Mild-moderate (outpatient): IM Ceftriaxone 1g single dose + Doxycycline 100mg BD × 14 days + Metronidazole 400mg BD × 14 days
  • Severe (admit): IV Cefoxitin 2g QDS + IV Doxycycline 100mg BD, then switch to oral after 24h
  • Partner notification and sexual health referral
4

Ovarian / Testicular Torsion

Gynaecology / urology surgical emergency. Theatre within 4-6h (ideally <6h for testicular torsion — detorsion possible up to 6h, salvage rate >90%). Do not delay for imaging if clinical suspicion high.

5

Threatened Miscarriage (β-hCG+, cervical os closed, IUP seen)

Anti-D if Rh negative + bleeding. Emotional support. Early pregnancy unit follow-up. Repeat USS in 7-14 days.

🚨 Cauda Equina Syndrome: Saddle anaesthesia + bladder/bowel dysfunction = SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Urgent MRI spine (same day). Neurosurgical referral immediately.
1

Cauda Equina Syndrome

Urgent MRI lumbar spine (same-day). Neurosurgery referral. Dexamethasone 8mg IV. Consider catheterisation if urinary retention. Do NOT discharge.

2

Suspected Spinal Infection (Epidural Abscess / Osteomyelitis)

Urgent MRI spine. Blood cultures ×2 before antibiotics. Flucloxacillin 2g QDS IV + Ceftriaxone 2g BD IV (empirical — adjust when sensitivities known). Neurosurgery/spinal surgery review.

3

Suspected Malignant Cord Compression

Dexamethasone 16mg PO/IV stat (NICE guideline). MRI whole spine. Oncology/neurosurgery referral. Radiotherapy vs surgery.

4

Aortic Dissection / Ruptured AAA

See relevant protocols. POCUS aorta immediately. Vascular surgery emergency.

5

Mechanical / MSK Back Pain (no red flags)

  • Paracetamol 1g QDS regular (first line)
  • Ibuprofen 400mg TDS + PPI (add if no contraindication) — more effective than paracetamol for acute MSK
  • Diazepam 2-5mg TDS (short course ≤5 days for muscle spasm) — caution dependence
  • Avoid bed rest. Keep mobile. Physiotherapy referral. NICE NG59: no imaging for non-specific LBP <6 weeks.

1

Haemodynamically Unstable

Massive haemorrhage protocol. O⁻ blood. IV ×2. Call gynaecology immediately. Theatre if ectopic or PPH.

2

All Rh-Negative Pregnant Patients with Bleeding

Anti-D immunoglobulin 250IU IM (≤20 weeks) or 500IU IM (>20 weeks). Do not withhold.

3

Threatened Miscarriage (os closed, FH present, <20wk)

Reassurance. Anti-D if Rh-negative. Refer to Early Pregnancy Unit (EPU) for follow-up USS. Avoid intercourse until reviewed. Return if heavy bleeding/pain.

4

Incomplete Miscarriage

Gynaecology review. Options: expectant / Misoprostol 800mcg vaginal / surgical (ERPC). Anti-D.

5

Septic Abortion

Resuscitate. Blood cultures. Co-amoxiclav 1.2g IV TDS + Metronidazole 500mg IV TDS. Gynaecology for surgical evacuation. ITU if septic shock.

6

Post-Menopausal Bleeding

Urgent (2-week wait) gynaecology referral. TVUS + endometrial biopsy. Must exclude endometrial carcinoma.

7

Heavy Non-Pregnant Bleeding (AUB)

  • If haemodynamically unstable: Tranexamic acid 1g IV TDS (may repeat at 6-8h)
  • High-dose oestrogen: Norethisterone 5mg TDS (acute hormonal control)
  • Gynaecology referral for definitive management

Conjunctivitis (bacterial)Chloramphenicol 0.5% drops QDS × 5 days. Hygiene advice.GP if no improvement in 5 days

PATTERN OF JOINT INVOLVEMENT:
□ Monoarthritis: one joint (septic arthritis / gout / pseudogout / trauma / haemarthrosis)
□ Migratory arthritis: one joint then another (reactive arthritis, gonococcal, rheumatic fever)
□ Additive polyarthritis: joints accumulate (RA, psoriatic, seronegative)
□ Symmetric small joints: RA (MCPs, PIPs, wrists), avoid DIPs
□ Asymmetric large joints: seronegative (SpA)
□ 1st MTP: gout (podagra)

ASSOCIATED FEATURES:
□ Fever / rigors (septic arthritis)
□ Preceding trauma / surgery
□ Recent infection (urogenital / GI — reactive arthritis 2-4 wks prior)
□ Skin rash: psoriasis / erythema migrans / gonococcal pustules
□ Eye symptoms: uveitis / conjunctivitis (seronegative / reactive)
□ Urogenital: urethral discharge / dysuria (gonococcal / reactive)
□ Oral ulcers (SLE / Behçet's)
□ Raynaud's phenomenon
□ Subcutaneous nodules / tophi (gout)

□ Recent intra-articular injection   □ Skin / wound infection

ARTHROCENTESIS (aspiration) — mandatory if septic arthritis possible:
Appearance: clear / turbid / bloody / haemorrhagic
WBC: ___/mm³   [normal <200; OA <2000; inflammatory <75,000; septic >50,000]
Crystals: gout (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent) / CPPD (rhomboid, positively birefringent)

Most likely: ___________________________________________
Septic arthritis excluded: Y / N / uncertain
🚨 Septic Arthritis: Hot, swollen joint + fever → joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics. Do NOT delay treatment. Prosthetic joint = orthopaedic emergency.
1

Septic Arthritis

  • Aspirate joint before antibiotics (send for MC&S, WBC, crystals)
  • Empirical: Flucloxacillin 2g IV QDS (MSSA) + consider Gentamicin if Gram-negative risk
  • MRSA risk: Vancomycin IV (per local protocol)
  • Gonococcal: Ceftriaxone 1g IV OD
  • Orthopaedics: surgical washout often required (hip/shoulder mandatory)
  • Admit. Splint for comfort. Physiotherapy once infection controlled.
2

Gout

  • Do NOT start allopurinol during acute flare (can prolong/worsen)
  • First-line: Naproxen 500mg BD (or Indomethacin 50mg TDS) + PPI if >65/NSAID risk
  • If NSAIDs contraindicated: Colchicine 500mcg BD–TDS (or 1mg stat then 500mcg 1h later)
  • Steroids if NSAIDs + colchicine contraindicated: Prednisolone 30-35mg OD × 5 days
  • Ice packs, joint rest, hydration. Dietary advice: avoid red meat/offal, alcohol, high-fructose foods.
3

Pseudogout (CPPD)

Aspiration (diagnostic + therapeutic). NSAIDs or colchicine (same as gout). Treat underlying metabolic cause (hyperPTH, haemochromatosis).

4

Reactive Arthritis

NSAIDs. Treat underlying infection if still active. Refer rheumatology. HLA-B27 testing.

Anaphylaxis

EMERGENCY — TREAT FIRST
💊 Treatment Protocol
📋 History Template
🚨 TREAT FIRST. History and examination are secondary to immediate adrenaline.
StepActionDrug / Dose
1 — ImmediateCall for help. Remove/stop trigger if possible. Position: supine + legs raised (or sitting if resp distress). Give adrenaline IM.Adrenaline 500mcg IM (0.5ml of 1:1000) anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5 min if no improvement.
2 — AirwayHigh-flow O₂. Senior airway help early if stridor/angioedema — may need early RSI (ketamine preferred).O₂ 15L/min NRB
3 — IV Access + FluidsLarge-bore IV ×2. Fluid bolus if hypotensive.500ml–1L crystalloid IV rapidly. Repeat as needed.
4 — AntihistamineFor urticaria/pruritus (adjunct — does NOT treat airway/circulatory compromise).Chlorphenamine 10mg IV/IM
5 — CorticosteroidReduces risk of biphasic reaction (effect delayed 4-6h).Hydrocortisone 200mg IV/IM
6 — RefractoryIf adrenaline IM not working: adrenaline infusion. For wheeze: salbutamol nebs. β-blocker patient: glucagon.Adrenaline 0.5–1mg/h IV infusion (titrate). Salbutamol 5mg neb. Glucagon 1-2mg IV if on β-blockers.
7 — MonitoringMonitor for ≥6h (12h if severe/biphasic risk). Observe in resus.Continuous cardiac monitoring, SpO2, BP q15min

Discharge Checklist

  • □ Minimum 6h observation (12h if severe or poor follow-up)
  • □ Allergy referral (NICE NG80) — refer all after confirmed anaphylaxis
  • □ Two EpiPens prescribed (Adrenaline 0.3mg auto-injector) with training
  • □ MedicAlert bracelet discussed
  • □ Trigger identified and documented — patient counselled to avoid
  • □ Written anaphylaxis action plan given
  • □ GP letter sent

Ipratropium 0.5mg neb q4-6h		Hydrocortisone 100mg IV or prednisolone POIV access. VBG. CXR.
Life-threateningHigh-flow O₂Continuous salbutamol. IV if nebuliser not effective: Salbutamol 5mcg/min IV infusionHydrocortisone 100mg QDS IVMgSO₄ 2g IV over 20 min (once). Call anaesthetics. ITU.
⚠️ Discharge criteria (BTS): PEFR >75% predicted, minimal symptoms, SpO2 >94%, stable for 1h after last bronchodilator. Discharge with written action plan, SABA, oral steroids (5-day course), step-up of preventer, GP review in 2 days, respiratory clinic F/U.
+

Intubation (Last Resort)

  • Ketamine is agent of choice (bronchodilator): Ketamine 1-2mg/kg IV
  • Rocuronium 1.2mg/kg IV (avoid suxamethonium — hyperkalaemia risk in severe asthma)
  • Low RR (6-10 bpm), long expiratory time (I:E = 1:3 or 1:4), low TV (6ml/kg)
  • Accept permissive hypercapnia

Home O₂: Y/N (flow rate: ___ L/min)   Previous NIV: Y/N   Previous ICU/intubation: Y/N

EXAMINATION:
Appearance: comfortable / pursed-lip breathing / accessory muscles / tripod position
Chest: barrel-shaped: Y/N   Hyperresonant: Y/N
Breath sounds: globally reduced / wheeze / crackles
JVP: elevated Y/N   Ankle oedema: Y/N
Signs of CO₂ retention: bounding pulse / asterixis / drowsiness / flushed
Cyanosis: Y/N

Severity: mild / moderate / severe
Type II respiratory failure: Y/N
Antibiotic indication: Y/N (Anthonisen criteria met: ___)
1

Controlled Oxygen (CRITICAL)

Target SpO2 88-92%. Use Venturi mask (24% or 28% to start). Avoid high-flow O₂ — risk of CO₂ retention. Recheck VBG 30-60 min after O₂ change.

2

Bronchodilators

  • Salbutamol 2.5-5mg neb q4-6h (can give back-to-back if severe)
  • Ipratropium 500mcg neb q6h (add to salbutamol)
  • MDI via spacer equally effective if patient can cooperate
3

Corticosteroids

Prednisolone 30mg PO OD × 5 days (NICE NG115). IV if oral route not possible: Hydrocortisone 100mg QDS.

4

Antibiotics (if ≥2 Anthonisen or clinical infection)

  • First-line: Amoxicillin 500mg TDS PO × 5 days
  • Penicillin allergy / purulent sputum / failure: Doxycycline 200mg stat then 100mg OD × 5 days
  • Complicated / hospital-acquired / Pseudomonas risk: Co-amoxiclav 625mg TDS or Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD
5

NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) — if pH <7.35 + pCO₂ >6kPa

  • BiPAP: start IPAP 12-16cmH₂O / EPAP 4-6cmH₂O, titrate SpO2 to 88-92%
  • Regular VBG monitoring (30 min, 1h, 2h post-NIV commencement)
  • If NIV fails or contraindicated → ITU + intubation (discuss ceiling of care)
⚠️ Discuss ceiling of care / DNACPR with senior if severe exacerbation with co-morbidities. Document clearly.

STEMI / NSTEMI / Unstable Angina / Low-risk chest pain

1

Immediate — All ACS

  • IV access, 12-lead ECG within 10 min, continuous monitoring, O₂ only if SpO2 <94%
  • Aspirin 300mg PO (chewed/dispersible) — give immediately
  • GTN 400mcg SL q5min (avoid if SBP<90, RV infarct, PDE5 inhibitor use)
  • Morphine 2–5mg IV titrated + Metoclopramide 10mg IV if pain not controlled
2

STEMI — PPCI Pathway (NICE NG185)

  • Call cardiology immediately. Target door-to-balloon <90 min.
  • Ticagrelor 180mg PO — preferred P2Y12 inhibitor (avoid if prior haemorrhagic stroke, on anticoagulation with high bleeding risk)
  • Or Prasugrel 60mg PO (PCI only; avoid if age >75, <60kg, prior stroke/TIA)
  • UFH 5000 IU IV bolus (or per cardiology protocol)
  • If PPCI >120 min away: Tenecteplase (TNKase) IV — weight-based (30-50mg) + Enoxaparin
3

NSTEMI/UA — Risk Stratification (NICE NG185)

  • Aspirin 300mg PO then 75mg OD
  • Ticagrelor 180mg PO then 90mg BD (unless very high bleeding risk)
  • Fondaparinux 2.5mg SC (anticoagulation of choice unless immediate angiography — use UFH/bivalirudin instead)
  • GRACE score >140 or refractory ischaemia → invasive strategy within 24h
  • GRACE score ≤140 but troponin rise → within 72h
4

RV Infarct (inferior STEMI + hypotension)

  • AVOID: nitrates, diuretics, morphine (preload-dependent)
  • IV fluid challenge: 250ml N/saline IV bolus — reassess; may need 1-2L
  • Dopamine/noradrenaline if persistent hypotension
  • Urgent PPCI
5

Cardiogenic Shock (Killip IV)

  • Urgent PPCI + cardiogenic shock team activation
  • Noradrenaline 0.05–0.3mcg/kg/min (vasopressor) + Dobutamine 2.5–10mcg/kg/min (inotrope)
  • Consider IABP / Impella / ECMO (specialist centre)

🚨 SCAPE: Sudden onset + hypertensive + flash pulmonary oedema — high-dose GTN infusion is first-line, not diuretics
1

Immediate — All Acute HF

  • Sit upright, high-flow O₂ (target SpO2 94-98%), IV access, continuous monitoring
  • CPAP 5-10cmH₂O (NICE — reduces intubation rate in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, NNT ~8)
  • Treat precipitant: rate control for AF, antibiotics for infection, ACS pathway, etc.
2

Wet + Warm (Euvolaemic overload)

  • Furosemide IV: if on oral furosemide — double their daily dose as IV. If furosemide-naïve: 40–80mg IV
  • GTN 0.4mg SL q5min if SBP >110 (add GTN infusion if persistent)
  • Monitor urine output (Foley catheter)
3

SCAPE (Hypertensive Pulmonary Oedema)

  • CPAP immediately
  • High-dose GTN infusion: start 100-200mcg/min IV, titrate up to 400mcg/min (far higher than usual — this is the SCAPE protocol, Grey Book and ESC endorsed)
  • Smaller diuretic dose or none initially — these patients are often not fluid overloaded
4

Wet + Cold (Cardiogenic Shock — SBP <90)

  • Do NOT use GTN or diuretics
  • Noradrenaline 0.05–0.3mcg/kg/min IV (vasopressor — restore MAP >65)
  • If low output dominant: add Dobutamine 2.5–10mcg/kg/min IV (inotrope)
  • Urgent cardiology — consider IABP / mechanical support
5

Renal Monitoring

U&E 4-6h post-diuresis. Acceptable: Cr rise <25% or <44μmol/L. Stop ACEi temporarily if AKI develops. Target urine output >0.5ml/kg/h.

  □ Haemoptysis   □ Syncope / presyncope
  □ Tachycardia   □ Hypotension

RISK FACTORS (CLOTS):
C — Cancer (active / treated within 6 months)
L — Long journey / Immobility (>3 days bedrest / flight >4h)
O — OCP / HRT / testosterone / pregnancy / postpartum
T — Trauma / surgery (especially orthopaedic) within 4 weeks
S — Stasis (previous DVT/PE / thrombophilia / obesity / CCF)

Additional: □ Leg cast   □ Central venous catheter   □ Dehydration

DVT WELLS SCORE:
□ Active malignancy                                          +1
□ Paralysis/paresis or recent immobilisation                 +1
□ Bedridden >3 days OR major surgery last 12 weeks          +1
□ Localised tenderness along deep venous system             +1
□ Entire leg swollen                                         +1
□ Calf swelling >3cm vs asymptomatic side                   +1
□ Pitting oedema (symptomatic leg)                          +1
□ Collateral superficial veins (non-varicose)               +1
□ Previously documented DVT                                 +1
□ Alternative diagnosis at least as likely                  -2
DVT Wells Total: ___   [<2 = DVT unlikely; ≥2 = DVT likely]

PE WELLS SCORE:
□ Clinical signs/symptoms of DVT                           +3
□ PE more likely than alternative diagnosis                +3
□ Heart rate >100 bpm                                      +1.5
□ Immobilisation ≥3 days or surgery in past 4 weeks       +1.5
□ Previous DVT or PE                                       +1.5
□ Haemoptysis                                              +1
□ Active malignancy (treatment within 6 months)            +1
PE Wells Total: ___   [≤4 = PE unlikely; >4 = PE likely]

PERC RULE (apply if PE Wells ≤4 AND pre-test probability LOW):
All must be absent to rule out PE without D-dimer:
□ Age ≥50   □ HR ≥100   □ SpO2 <95%   □ Haemoptysis
□ Oestrogen use   □ Prior PE/DVT   □ Unilateral leg swelling
□ Recent surgery/trauma (≤4 weeks)
PERC negative (all absent): Y/N → if yes, no further PE workup needed

YEARS ALGORITHM (alternative to Wells + PERC in UK — NICE NG158):
□ Clinical signs of DVT (Y/N)
□ Haemoptysis (Y/N)
□ PE most likely diagnosis (Y/N)
0 YEARS items: D-dimer <1000 μg/L excludes PE
≥1 YEARS items: D-dimer <500 μg/L excludes PE

AGE-ADJUSTED D-DIMER (>50 years):
Threshold = age × 10 μg/L (e.g., 65 years → <650 μg/L = negative)

INVESTIGATIONS:
D-dimer: ___ μg/L (normal <500, or age-adjusted)
CTPA result: ___________________________
Leg Doppler USS: ___________________________
ECG: sinus tach / AF / S1Q3T3 / new RBBB / T-wave inversion V1-4 / right axis
CXR: normal / Hampton's hump / Westermark sign / pleural effusion
Echo/POCUS: RV dilatation Y/N   RV/LV ratio >0.9 Y/N   McConnell's sign Y/N
Troponin: ___   BNP: ___

IMPRESSION:
DVT: confirmed / suspected / excluded
PE: massive / high risk / intermediate-high / intermediate-low / low / excluded

YEARS Algorithm (NICE NG158 — UK Standard)

YEARS items presentD-dimer thresholdAction
0 YEARS items<1000 μg/LPE excluded — no CTPA
0 YEARS items≥1000 μg/LCTPA
≥1 YEARS item<500 μg/LPE excluded — no CTPA
≥1 YEARS item≥500 μg/LCTPA

YEARS items: ① Clinical DVT signs ② Haemoptysis ③ PE most likely diagnosis. Age-adjusted D-dimer can be applied to the ≥1 YEARS arm in patients >50.

sPESI Score (for PE severity / safe discharge)

VariablePoints
Age >80+1
Cancer+1
Chronic cardiopulmonary disease+1
HR ≥110+1
SBP <100mmHg+1
SpO2 <90%+1

sPESI = 0 → low risk (30-day mortality ~1%) — consider outpatient DOAC management if no other barriers. sPESI ≥1 → admit.

1

Massive PE (haemodynamically unstable)

  • Call resus team. POCUS (RV strain). ABCs.
  • Alteplase 50mg IV bolus (thrombolysis — if no absolute contraindication)
  • If thrombolysis fails/contraindicated: surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy
  • If cardiac arrest: CPR + Alteplase 50mg IV, continue CPR 60-90 min
2

Intermediate-High Risk PE (haemodynamically stable + RV strain)

  • Anticoagulate immediately. Close monitoring — ICU/HDU.
  • Rescue thrombolysis if haemodynamic deterioration
3

Non-Massive PE — Anticoagulation (NICE NG158)

  • First-line: Apixaban 10mg BD × 7 days then 5mg BD
  • Or Rivaroxaban 15mg BD × 21 days then 20mg OD
  • Active cancer: Apixaban or Rivaroxaban preferred over LMWH (newer evidence)
  • Pregnancy: LMWH (dalteparin) SC — no DOACs
  • Renal impairment (eGFR <15): UFH infusion
4

DVT Anticoagulation

  • Proximal DVT: anticoagulate as per PE above (DOACs preferred)
  • Distal DVT (below-knee): consider anticoagulation or surveillance USS in 1 week (if low-risk)
  • Duration: 3 months (provoked); 6 months+ (unprovoked — discuss with haematology)
5

Low-Risk PE — Outpatient (NICE NG158)

  • sPESI = 0, no contraindication, reliable patient, confirmed PE
  • DOAC prescribed, follow-up arranged within 48-72h
  • Written information, safety netting (return if worse)
⚠️ All first unprovoked PE/DVT: investigate for underlying malignancy (history, exam, FBC, CXR, urinalysis). Consider thrombophilia screen (6 weeks after anticoagulation stopped).

Immediate — All Stroke (NICE NG128)

  • Check CBG immediately (exclude hypoglycaemia)

  • IV access, bloods: FBC, U&E, coagulation, group & save, glucose, lipids
  • 12-lead ECG (AF?)
  • Swallow screen before any oral intake (water swallow test by nurse or SLT)
2

Thrombolysis (if eligible, CT haemorrhage excluded, within 4.5h)

  • Alteplase 0.9mg/kg IV (max 90mg): 10% as IV bolus, remainder over 60 min
  • BP target before thrombolysis: <185/110mmHg. Use Labetalol 10-20mg IV to lower if needed
  • Post-thrombolysis: BP <180/105 for 24h, no antiplatelets for 24h, no NGT/catheter for 30 min
  • Monitor neurologically every 15 min for 2h
3

Thrombectomy (if eligible — NICE TA524)

  • Within 6h of onset (or up to 24h in selected wake-up/late-window patients)
  • Refer immediately to thrombectomy centre
  • Can be given alongside thrombolysis (bridging)
4

Antiplatelet Therapy (ischaemic stroke/TIA)

  • If thrombolysis given: start Aspirin 300mg OD after 24h (CT repeat to exclude haemorrhagic transformation first)
  • If no thrombolysis: Aspirin 300mg PO immediately
  • Dual antiplatelet (DAPT) for minor stroke/TIA: Aspirin 300mg + Clopidogrel 300mg stat then 75mg OD + Aspirin 75mg OD × 21 days (POINT trial — NICE supported)
5

BP Management

  • Do NOT lower BP acutely in ischaemic stroke (unless thrombolysis or SBP >220)
  • Permissive hypertension — allows collateral flow
  • Haemorrhagic stroke: target SBP <140 within 1h (use Labetalol IV)
6

TIA — ABCD² Score + Urgent Management

  • ABCD² ≥4 or AF suspected or crescendo TIA → admit / urgent assessment within 24h
  • Start Aspirin 300mg immediately
  • DAPT as above if minor stroke/TIA
  • MRI brain, Carotid Doppler, 24h ECG (AF?), echo (if cardioembolic source suspected)
  • Carotid endarterectomy within 2 weeks if 50-99% symptomatic stenosis

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE NG128 — Stroke and TIA in Over 16s (2019) ↗ ROSIER Scale — Nor et al., Lancet Neurology 2005 ↗ ABCD² Score — Johnston et al., Lancet 2007 ↗ NIHSS Stroke Scale

Treatment Targets (DKA resolution — JBDS)

✅ Glucose <14mmol/L within 6h

✅ Bicarbonate rising by ≥3mmol/L/h
✅ pH rising (target >7.3)

HHS Specific Points

  • Rehydrate MORE SLOWLY than DKA (correct over 24-48h, not 12h — rapid correction risks cerebral oedema)

  • Insulin: only start insulin if ketones >1mmol/L OR glucose not falling with fluids alone
  • LMWH prophylaxis: high thrombosis risk — (eg SC OD Dalterparin) unless contraindicated
  • Target: reduce serum osmolality by 3-8mOsm/kg/h

🚨 SEPSIS 6 — Complete ALL within 1 HOUR (NICE NG253, UK Sepsis Trust)

The Sepsis 6 (within 1 hour)

#ActionDetail
1🩸 Blood cultures≥2 sets from different sites before antibiotics. Also: urine MC&S, sputum, wound swabs as appropriate.
2💉 IV antibioticsWithin 1h (within 3h for non-septic shock). Broad-spectrum per local policy. Unknown source: Piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5g IV TDS ± Gentamicin 5mg/kg IV (level-guided). Neutropenic: add antifungal. CNS: add Ceftriaxone 2g BD.
3💧 IV fluids500ml crystalloid (Hartmann's or 0.9% NaCl) IV bolus — repeat if hypotensive. Target MAP ≥65, cap refill ≤2s, lactate clearance. Reassess after each bolus (POCUS if available). Max ~30ml/kg unless cardiogenic cause.
4🔴 LactateMeasure (VBG). Lactate >4 = septic shock → HDU/ITU. Remeasure at 1h and 6h. Target: clearance ≥10%/h.
5💛 Urine outputCatheterise. Target ≥0.5ml/kg/h. If oliguric despite fluids → escalate.
6🌬️ OxygenTarget SpO2 94-98% (88-92% if COPD). High-flow O₂ initially, then titrate.
+

Vasopressors (if MAP <65 despite 2L fluids)

  • Noradrenaline 0.01–0.5mcg/kg/min IV via central line (or peripheral line temporarily)
  • Add Vasopressin 0.03 units/min if noradrenaline >0.25mcg/kg/min
  • Hydrocortisone (if refractory shock): Hydrocortisone 50mg IV QDS
+

Source Control

Identify and control source urgently: drain abscess, remove infected device/line, surgical review for peritonitis/necrotising fasciitis, ERCP for cholangitis

⚠️ Antibiotic stewardship: Review and de-escalate antibiotics at 24-48h based on culture results and clinical response. Stop if no infection confirmed. Document indication and planned stop date.

Upper / Lower GIB
Suspected source: ___________________________________________
GBS: ___   Severity: mild / moderate / severe / haemodynamic compromise
1

Resuscitation

  • Large-bore IV × 2. Blood group and crossmatch.
  • 0.9% NaCl 500ml IV bolus — bridge until blood available
  • Massive haemorrhage protocol if shocked: O-negative pRBC + FFP + platelets (1:1:1)
  • Tranexamic acid 1g IV (consider within 3h of GI bleed onset — evidence emerging)
  • Hb transfusion threshold: <70 g/L (or <80 g/L in IHD). Target 70-90 g/L.
2

Upper GI Bleed — PUD

  • IV PPI (omeprazole 80mg bolus then 8mg/h infusion) — start pre-endoscopy if suspected PUD
  • Urgent OGD within 24h (within 12h if haemodynamically unstable)
  • NBM from midnight (or 4h before anticipated endoscopy)
3

Variceal Bleeding (liver disease + haematemesis)

  • Terlipressin 2mg IV QDS (reduces splanchnic blood flow) — start immediately, continue 5 days
  • Ceftriaxone 1g IV OD × 5 days (antibiotic prophylaxis — reduces mortality)
  • Urgent OGD (band ligation) within 12h
  • If bleeding uncontrolled: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube as bridge (specialist only)
  • Vitamin K 10mg IV if coagulopathic (INR >1.5); FFP/PCC if actively bleeding
4

Anticoagulation Reversal

  • Warfarin: Vitamin K 5-10mg IV + Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) for urgent reversal
  • DOAC: discuss with haematology; idarucizumab for dabigatran
  • Restart anticoagulation when haemostasis achieved (usually 7-14 days — balance risk of thrombosis)
5

Low-Risk (GBS = 0)

Consider outpatient management with next-day endoscopy. Safety net: return immediately if haematemesis, melaena, presyncope, or worsening. GP follow-up.

⚠️ H. pylori testing: All PUD bleeds should have CLO test or breath test. Treat if positive (triple therapy). Avoid NSAIDs + add PPI if restart.

ℹ️ Identify the toxidrome first — guides empiric treatment before specific identification
ToxidromeCausesFeaturesTreatment
OpioidMorphine, codeine, fentanyl, heroin, methadone, tramadolMiosis, CNS depression, respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypothermiaNaloxone 400mcg IV/IM/IN — titrate. Infusion if long-acting opioid.
AnticholinergicTCAs, antihistamines, hyoscine, antipsychotics, atropine"Mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, hot as a hare" — mydriasis, tachycardia, dry skin, urinary retention, ileus, hyperthermia, confusionSupportive. Physostigmine only specialist use. Benzos for agitation.
CholinergicOrganophosphates, nerve agents, carbamylSLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI distress, Emesis + bradycardia, bronchospasm, miosis, seizuresAtropine 2-4mg IV q5min until secretions dry. Pralidoxime 1-2g IV (within 24h).
SympathomimeticCocaine, amphetamines, MDMA, ephedrineMydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, agitation, sweating, seizuresBenzos for agitation/seizures. Avoid beta-blockers. Cooling. GTN for HTN.
Serotonin SyndromeSSRIs + MAOIs, tramadol, fentanyl, lithium, linezolidHunter triad: clonus + agitation + diaphoresis. Hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, tachycardia.Stop offending drug. Cyproheptadine 8mg PO. Benzos. Active cooling. ICU if severe.
Sedative-HypnoticBenzos, barbiturates, alcohol, GHB, z-drugsCNS depression, normal pupils, normal vitals (unlike opioids), ataxiaSupportive airway management. Flumazenil 200mcg IV only if benzo-naïve (risk of seizures in chronic use).
1

Paracetamol Overdose (MHRA/TOXBASE)

  • Activated charcoal 50g PO if within 1h of ingestion (and airway safe)
  • Paracetamol level at 4h post-ingestion — plot on Rumack-Matthew nomogram
  • If above treatment line OR staggered/unknown timing: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)
  • NAC regimen (MHRA 2-bag): NAC 200mg/kg in 200ml 5% glucose over 4h, then NAC 100mg/kg in 1000ml 5% glucose over 16h
  • Check LFTs, INR, creatinine at end of 2nd bag. Continue if ALT elevated.
  • High-risk criteria (liver enzyme inducers, malnutrition, anorexia, alcohol): lower treatment threshold
2

Opioid Overdose

  • Naloxone 400mcg IV/IM/IN — titrate to adequate respiration (not full reversal — avoid precipitating withdrawal)
  • Repeat 400mcg every 2-3 min up to 2mg if no response
  • Long-acting opioid (methadone, buprenorphine): naloxone infusion (⅔ of effective bolus dose per hour)
  • Duration of action: naloxone 30-90 min vs opioid often hours — observe minimum 4-6h
3

Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Overdose

  • QRS >100ms = risk of arrhythmia. QRS >160ms = high risk VT/VF.
  • Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50-100ml IV bolus — for QRS widening or arrhythmia (aim serum pH 7.45-7.55)
  • Benzos for seizures. Avoid phenytoin (pro-arrhythmic in TCA OD).
  • Avoid physostigmine. Avoid flumazenil if co-ingested benzo (lowers seizure threshold).
  • Intubate early if GCS declining. ICU.
4

Salicylate (Aspirin) Overdose

  • Levels: mild <300mg/L / moderate 300-700mg/L / severe >700mg/L
  • VBG: respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis (mixed)
  • IV fluids + Urine alkalinisation: Sodium bicarbonate 1-2mmol/kg IV (target urine pH 7.5-8.5) — enhances urinary excretion
  • Haemodialysis if: level >700mg/L, renal failure, severe acidosis, pulmonary oedema, CNS effects
5

Beta-Blocker / Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose

  • Atropine for bradycardia (often ineffective): Atropine 600mcg-3mg IV
  • Glucagon 5-10mg IV bolus then infusion (beta-blocker reversal)
  • High-dose insulin euglycaemia (HDIE): Insulin 1 unit/kg/h IV + glucose 10% infusion — evidence-based for CCB/BB toxicity
  • Lipid emulsion therapy: Intralipid 20% 1.5ml/kg IV bolus — for refractory cardiac toxicity (specialist use)
  • Transvenous pacing if pharmacological measures fail
6

CO Poisoning

  • COHb: correlate with symptoms (NOT reliable indicator of severity)
  • 100% O₂ via tight-fitting NRB mask — continue for minimum 6h (reduces COHb t½ from 5h to 60-90min)
  • Hyperbaric oxygen (HBO): discuss with National Poisons Centre (0344 892 0111) if: LOC, COHb >25%, pregnancy, cardiac symptoms, neurological features
  • ECG monitoring — CO causes myocardial injury
⚠️ TOXBASE: Always check TOXBASE (toxbase.org — NHS login) or call National Poisons Information Service 0344 892 0111 for specific management guidance.

Psychiatric Emergencies

Rapid Tranquillisation (NICE NG10)

StepAgentDoseNotes
1st — Oral offerLorazepam PO or Olanzapine ODTLorazepam 1-2mg PO / Olanzapine 10mg ODTAlways offer oral first. Document refusal.
2nd — IM (if oral refused)Lorazepam IM1-2mg IM (max 4mg in 24h)Can repeat after 30-60 min. Monitor resps.
IM alternativeHaloperidol IM5mg IM (2.5mg if elderly or antipsychotic-naïve)Monitor QTc. AVOID with olanzapine IM — risk fatal respiratory depression.
IM alternativeOlanzapine IM10mg IMDo NOT give IM olanzapine + IM/IV benzodiazepine together.
3rd — IV (resus setting)Midazolam IV2.5-5mg IV titratedAirway support on hand. Flumazenil available.

Post-RT monitoring: Pulse, BP, RR, SpO2 every 5-10 min for 1h then every 30 min. Resuscitation equipment at bedside. Flumazenil and naloxone available.

⚠️ Alcohol / substance intoxication: Reduce all RT doses significantly. Higher risk of respiratory depression. Avoid antipsychotics if possible. Lorazepam 0.5-1mg IM is preferred.
1

Medical Stabilisation First

Always treat medical consequences before psychiatric assessment. Paracetamol/salicylate levels in all DSH regardless of reported ingestion. Wound assessment and closure if laceration.

2

Risk Assessment

Use structured assessment (see proforma). High lethality of attempt, planned method, precautions to avoid discovery, persistent intent = HIGH RISK. Do not discharge without senior review and/or psychiatric liaison.

3

Psychiatric Liaison Referral

All deliberate self-harm should have a psychosocial assessment before discharge (NICE NG225). Contact psychiatric liaison team. If out of hours: on-call psychiatry / crisis team.

4

Safe Messaging + Discharge Safety Plan

  • Written safety plan: warning signs / coping strategies / support contacts / crisis numbers
  • Remove or limit access to means (discuss with family re medication safety)
  • Follow-up within 48-72h arranged before discharge
  • Samaritans: 116 123 (24/7). Crisis team number: ___
5

Capacity and MHA (if declining treatment)

If lacks capacity (acute mental illness affecting decision): treat in best interests. If has capacity but high risk: consider urgent MHA assessment (Section 2) via AMHP. Section 5(2) available to consultant/SpR to prevent leaving.

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE NG10 — Violence and Aggression: Short-Term Management in Mental Health (2015) ↗ NICE NG225 — Self-Harm: Assessment, Management and Preventing Recurrence (2022) ↗ Mental Health Act 1983 (amended 2007) ↗ Mental Capacity Act 2005 ↗ RCEM — Mental Health in Emergency Departments Toolkit

SYMPTOMS BY SYSTEM:
□ HEENT: ear pain / otorrhoea / sore throat / cervical lymphadenopathy / rhinorrhoea
□ Respiratory: cough (duration/character) / wheeze / stridor / increased WOB
□ GI: vomiting / diarrhoea / abdominal pain / feeding change
□ GU: dysuria / frequency / haematuria (urine dip + MC&S in all <2yrs with fever)
□ Neuro: seizure (febrile vs. epileptic) / headache / photophobia / neck stiffness
□ Skin: rash (type and distribution — see below)
□ MSK: joint swelling / reluctance to weight bear / bone tenderness

RASH ASSESSMENT:
□ Petechial / purpuric (non-blanching) → meningococcal until proven otherwise
□ Blanching maculopapular → viral exanthem (measles, rubella, roseola, scarlet fever)
□ Vesicular → varicella / herpes
□ Urticarial → allergic
□ Target lesions → erythema multiforme / Lyme
□ Strawberry tongue + desquamation → Kawasaki / scarlet fever

NON-BLANCHING RASH — IMMEDIATE ACTION:
Any non-blanching rash + fever = meningococcal septicaemia until proven otherwise
→ IM/IV Benzylpenicillin IMMEDIATELY (see management)

Post-ictal: Y/N   Duration: ___   Back to baseline: Y/N

□ Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis
□ Polymorphous rash
□ Cervical lymphadenopathy (≥1.5cm)
□ Changes in lips/oral mucosa (strawberry tongue, red cracked lips)
□ Changes in extremities (erythema / oedema / desquamation)

NICE NG143 Traffic Light System

Feature🟢 Green (low risk)🟡 Amber (intermediate)🔴 Red (high risk)
ColourNormalPallor reported by parentPale/mottled/ashen/blue
ActivityNormal response, content, awake or easily rousable, strong cryNot responding normally, wakes with prolonged stimulation, decreased activityNo response to stimulation, AVPU <A, weak/high-pitched cry
RespiratoryNormalRR >50 (<12mo), >40 (1-5yr), SpO2 <95% (air), nasal flare, cracklesGrunting, RR >60, moderate-severe chest indrawing
Circulation/HydrationNormal skin and eyes, moist mucous membranesTachycardia, CRT ≥3s, dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output, poor feedingReduced skin turgor
OtherNo amber or red featuresFever ≥5 days, swelling limb/joint, non-weight bearing, new lump >2cmNon-blanching rash, bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, focal neurology, seizures, bile-stained vomiting
ActionDischarge with safety net adviceFurther assessment + bloods + possible admissionEmergency treatment + senior review + immediate bloods/imaging
⚠️ Age <3 months: Fever ≥38°C = RED flag — admit all regardless of clinical appearance. Age 3-6 months: ≥39°C or any amber feature = admit.
1

Non-Blanching Rash + Fever (Meningococcal)

  • Benzylpenicillin IV/IM immediately:
    <1yr: 300mg | 1-9yr: 600mg | ≥10yr: 1200mg
    Penicillin allergy: Ceftriaxone 80mg/kg IV (max 4g)
  • Resuscitate as sepsis. Call PICU. Inform PHE.
2

Antipyretics

  • Paracetamol 15mg/kg PO/IV q4-6h (max 4 doses/24h)
  • Ibuprofen 5-10mg/kg PO q6-8h (avoid if <3 months, dehydrated, asthma, or chickenpox)
  • Do NOT alternate routinely — only switch if one fails to control fever
3

Febrile Convulsion

  • Simple febrile convulsion (brief, generalised, age 6mo-5yr): reassurance, antipyretics
  • Prolonged (>5 min): Buccal midazolam 0.5mg/kg (max 10mg) — preferred prehospital/community
    IV access: Lorazepam 0.1mg/kg IV (max 4mg)
  • LP not routine after simple febrile convulsion if clinical picture benign
  • Reassure parents — does not cause epilepsy. 30-35% recurrence risk.
4

Kawasaki Disease

  • Refer paediatrics urgently
  • Aspirin 30-50mg/kg/day PO (anti-inflammatory dose) until afebrile, then 3-5mg/kg/day
  • IV Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 2g/kg over 10-12h (reduces coronary artery aneurysm risk)
  • Echo for coronary artery assessment
5

Septic Screen (<3 months or RED)

FBC, CRP, blood cultures, urine MC&S, CXR, LP (if meningism/unexplained fever <1 month). Empirical Cefotaxime 50mg/kg IV + Amoxicillin 50mg/kg IV (covers Listeria <3 months).

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE NG143 — Fever in Under 5s: Assessment and Initial Management (2019) ↗ NICE NG241 — Meningitis (Bacterial) and Meningococcal Disease ↗ NICE NG224 — Urinary Tract Infection in Under 16s (2022)

ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY ASSESSMENT
================================
AKI STAGING (KDIGO):
Stage 1: Cr rise ≥26μmol/L in 48h OR ≥1.5×baseline
Stage 2: Cr ≥2×baseline
Stage 3: Cr ≥3×baseline OR Cr ≥354μmol/L OR commenced on RRT
AKI Stage: ___   Baseline Cr: ___   Current Cr: ___   eGFR: ___

HYPERKALAEMIA ASSESSMENT (treat first if K >6.0):
K⁺: ___mmol/L   ECG changes: Y/N

SYMPTOMS:
□ Oliguria (<0.5ml/kg/h or <400ml/day) / anuria   Duration: ___
□ Frothy/dark urine   □ Haematuria   □ Oedema
□ Nausea/vomiting   □ Confusion   □ Breathlessness (fluid overload)

CAUSE ASSESSMENT (PRE/INTRA/POST-RENAL):
PRE-RENAL (hypovolaemia/hypoperfusion):
□ Fluid loss: vomiting / diarrhoea / haemorrhage / burns / excessive diuresis
□ Reduced intake   □ Sepsis / shock   □ Cardiac failure   □ NSAIDs + ACEi/ARB
□ Recent contrast exposure (CI-AKI)

INTRA-RENAL (parenchymal):
□ ATN — ischaemic (post-prerenal if prolonged) or nephrotoxic (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, contrast, cisplatin)
□ Glomerulonephritis (haematuria + proteinuria + oedema = nephritic syndrome)
□ Interstitial nephritis (drug reaction: NSAIDs, antibiotics, PPIs — triad: rash + fever + eosinophilia)
□ Rhabdomyolysis (dark urine, CK elevated)
□ Myeloma (protein gap, bone pain, elderly)

POST-RENAL (obstruction):
□ Urinary retention (palpable bladder / MSU)
□ Prostatic enlargement   □ Ureteric stone / calculus   □ Pelvic malignancy
□ Retroperitoneal fibrosis

NEPHROTOXIC DRUG SCREEN (STOP or HOLD):
□ NSAIDs     □ ACEi / ARBs   □ Metformin   □ Methotrexate
□ Aminoglycosides   □ Vancomycin   □ Contrast   □ Diuretics (if pre-renal)
□ DOACs / LMWH (dose-reduce/hold in AKI)   □ Lithium

PMHx: CKD (baseline Cr: ___)   DM   HTN   myeloma   prostate disease
Medications: ACEi / ARBs / NSAIDs / diuretics / antibiotics / contrast

EXAMINATION:
BP: ___/___   HR: ___   JVP: normal / elevated / not seen
Volume status: hypovolaemic / euvolaemic / fluid overloaded
Skin turgor: normal / reduced   Mucous membranes: moist / dry
Pitting oedema: Y/N   Bladder: palpable Y/N
Loin tenderness: Y/N

INVESTIGATIONS:
U&E: Na___  K___  Cl___  Bicarb___  Urea___  Cr___  Ca___  Phosphate___
eGFR: ___   Baseline Cr: ___   Peak Cr: ___
FBC   LFTs   CRP   Glucose   Albumin   Uric acid
Urine: dip (protein ___  blood ___)   MC&S   urinary Na (if pre-vs-intrarenal)
  Urine Na <20mmol/L = pre-renal (kidney holding Na)
  Urine Na >40mmol/L = intrarenal (tubular damage)
  Urine:plasma osmolality ratio <1.5 = intrarenal ATN
CK (rhabdomyolysis): ___   Myoglobin: ___
CXR (pulmonary oedema)   USS kidneys (obstruction, asymmetry, size)
ECG: hyperkalaemia features (tall T waves / widened QRS / sine wave)

IMPRESSION:
AKI Stage: ___   Cause: pre-renal / intrarenal / post-renal
Precipitant: ___________________________
Hyperkalaemia: Y/N — ECG changes: Y/N
⚠️ Treat hyperkalaemia immediately if K >6.0 or ECG changes regardless of K level
1

Hyperkalaemia Emergency (K >6.0 or ECG changes)

  • Calcium gluconate 10% 30ml (or 10ml calcium chloride 10%) IV over 5-10 min — cardiac membrane stabilisation. Repeat if ECG not improving. Does NOT lower K.
  • Salbutamol 10-20mg nebulised — shifts K into cells (onset 30 min)
  • Insulin-dextrose: Actrapid 10 units + 50ml 50% glucose (or 250ml 20% glucose) IV over 15 min — shifts K into cells. Monitor glucose q30min.
  • Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50ml IV — if metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1)
  • Calcium resonium 15g PO or Patiromer — eliminates K (onset hours to days)
  • If refractory: emergency haemodialysis — nephrology referral urgently
2

Pre-Renal AKI — Fluid Resuscitation

  • IV crystalloid if hypovolaemic: 500ml Hartmann's bolus, reassess, repeat
  • Monitor urine output (catheterise). Target ≥0.5ml/kg/h.
  • STOP NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs, diuretics temporarily
  • If sepsis-related: follow sepsis 6 protocol
3

Post-Renal — Relieve Obstruction

  • Urinary retention: catheterise immediately. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis (replace ½ of urine output with IV fluids).
  • Ureteric obstruction: urology referral. Urgent USS or CT KUB.
4

Rhabdomyolysis

  • Aggressive IV fluids: target urine output 200-300ml/h until myoglobinuria resolves
  • Urinary alkalinisation (controversial — discuss with nephrology)
  • Monitor CK, K⁺, Ca²⁺, urine output closely
5

Indications for Emergency Dialysis (AEIOU)

A — Acidosis (pH <7.1 refractory) | E — Electrolytes (K >6.5 refractory) | I — Intoxication (dialysable toxins) | O — Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory) | U — Uraemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding) → Urgent nephrology referral

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE NG148 — Acute Kidney Injury: Prevention, Detection and Management (2019) ↗ KDIGO — Clinical Practice Guideline for AKI (2012) ↗ NHS England — Think Kidneys: AKI Resources

IMPORTANT
🧂 Sodium

Hyponatraemia (Na <135 mmol/L)

HYPONATRAEMIA ASSESSMENT
=========================
Na⁺: ___ mmol/L   Severity: mild (130-134) / moderate (125-129) / severe (<125)
Onset: acute (<48h) / chronic (>48h / unknown)

SYMPTOMS:
□ Mild: nausea, malaise, headache, confusion
□ Moderate: vomiting, drowsiness, seizure risk
□ Severe: seizures, GCS <8, respiratory arrest
Symptomatic: Y/N   Seizure: Y/N

CAUSE (assess volume status):
Volume status: hypovolaemic / euvolaemic / hypervolaemic

HYPOVOLAEMIC (total body Na low):
□ GI losses (vomiting/diarrhoea)   □ Burns   □ Haemorrhage
□ Diuretic excess   □ Addison's disease

EUVOLAEMIC (total body Na normal — water excess):
□ SIADH (commonest): pneumonia / SCLC / CNS disease / drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide)
□ Hypothyroidism   □ Psychogenic polydipsia   □ Beer potomania

HYPERVOLAEMIC (total body Na high — more water than Na):
□ CCF   □ Liver cirrhosis   □ Nephrotic syndrome   □ AKI/CKD

SIADH DIAGNOSIS (all must be present):
□ Urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg   □ Urine Na >20 mmol/L
□ Euvolaemia   □ Serum osmolality <280 mOsm/kg   □ No hypothyroid/adrenal insufficiency

MANAGEMENT (NICE / Endocrine Society):
Acute severe (<48h + severe symptoms):
→ 3% NaCl 150ml IV over 20 min — can repeat twice, target Na rise 5mmol/L
→ ICU/HDU referral

Chronic or unknown onset:
→ Target correction: NO MORE THAN 8-10mmol/L per 24h (risk osmotic demyelination syndrome)
→ Treat underlying cause
→ SIADH: fluid restriction (500-1000ml/day), demeclocycline (chronic), tolvaptan (specialist)
→ Volume depletion: 0.9% NaCl
→ Hypervolaemic: fluid restriction + diuretics (CCF/cirrhosis)

MONITOR: Na q4-6h during correction. If correcting too fast — give DDAVP to slow.

Potassium Disturbances

HYPOKALAEMIA (K <3.5 mmol/L)
==============================
K⁺: ___   Severity: mild 3.0-3.5 / moderate 2.5-3.0 / severe <2.5
Mg²⁺: ___ (hypoMg causes refractory hypoK — replace Mg first)

SYMPTOMS: weakness / cramps / ileus / palpitations / polyuria
ECG: flat/inverted T waves / prominent U wave / ST depression / prolonged QU / VT risk
ECG changes: Y/N

CAUSES: vomiting / diarrhoea / diuretics (furosemide, thiazides) / laxative abuse
        Cushing's / Conn's / hypoMg / RTA / insulin / alkalosis / β2-agonists

TREATMENT:
Oral (mild/moderate, tolerating PO): Sando-K 2 tablets TDS (each = 12mmol K)
IV (severe/unable to take PO/ECG changes):
  Peripheral: KCl 40mmol in 1L NaCl over 4h (max 10mmol/h via peripheral line)
  Central (if K <2.5 or rapid correction needed): up to 20mmol/h with monitoring
Replace Mg: MgSO4 10mmol IV over 1h if Mg low
MONITOR: ECG continuously if severe. Recheck K 2-4h post-replacement.

HYPERKALAEMIA (K >5.5 mmol/L)
==============================
K⁺: ___   Severity: mild 5.5-6.0 / moderate 6.0-6.5 / severe >6.5
ECG: peaked T waves / PR prolongation / QRS widening / sine wave / VF
ECG changes: Y/N → treat immediately regardless of K level if ECG changes

CAUSES: AKI/CKD / ACEi+ARB / NSAIDs / K-sparing diuretics / Addison's
        Massive haemolysis / rhabdomyolysis / DKA / acidosis / beta-blockers

TREATMENT (see AKI section — hyperkalaemia protocol):
1. Stabilise: Calcium gluconate 10% 30ml IV (cardiac membrane protection)
2. Shift: Insulin-dextrose (10u + 50g glucose) + Salbutamol 10-20mg neb
3. Remove: Calcium resonium / Patiromer (PO) or haemodialysis

Calcium Disturbances

HYPERCALCAEMIA (corrected Ca >2.65 mmol/L)
==========================================
Corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 - albumin)
Corrected Ca: ___   Severity: mild <3.0 / moderate 3.0-3.5 / severe >3.5

SYMPTOMS (Bones, Stones, Groans, Moans, Psychic Overtones):
□ Bones: bone pain / fractures   □ Stones: renal calculi / nephrocalcinosis
□ Groans: nausea / vomiting / constipation / peptic ulcer
□ Moans: fatigue / weakness / polyuria / polydipsia
□ Psychic: confusion / depression / psychosis / reduced GCS

ECG: shortened QT interval, AV block, bradycardia

CAUSES (CHIMPANZEES):
Primary hyperparathyroidism (commonest outpatient)
Malignancy (commonest inpatient — bone mets, myeloma, PTHrP)
Others: sarcoid / TB / Vit D toxicity / thiazides / lithium / immobility / thyrotoxicosis

PTH (elevated → primary hyperPTH; suppressed → malignancy or Vit D excess)
PTH: ___   Vitamin D: ___   PTHrP: ___

TREATMENT:
1. IV fluids: 0.9% NaCl 250-500ml/h — FIRST LINE (volume expansion + calciuresis)
   Target urine output 100-150ml/h. Avoid frusemide (no longer recommended routinely).
2. Bisphosphonates (once hydrated): Zoledronic acid 4mg IV over 15 min OR Pamidronate 60-90mg IV over 2-4h
   Onset: 48-72h. Duration: 3-4 weeks.
3. Denosumab (if renal failure, Ca extremely high)
4. Calcitonin 4-8 IU/kg SC/IM q12h — rapid onset (hours) but short-lived (tachyphylaxis)
5. Hydrocortisone 200mg IV — if sarcoidosis / Vit D toxicity / haematological malignancy
6. Dialysis: life-threatening hypercalcaemia + renal failure

HYPOCALCAEMIA (corrected Ca <2.1 mmol/L)
==========================================
Corrected Ca: ___   Mg²⁺: ___ (correct Mg first)
Symptoms: perioral/fingertip tingling / muscle cramps / tetany / Trousseau's sign / Chvostek's sign / seizures / prolonged QT
ECG: prolonged QT ___ms

CAUSES: hypoparathyroidism / hypoMg / Vit D deficiency / pancreatitis / CKD / post-thyroidectomy / rhabdomyolysis

TREATMENT:
Symptomatic / severe (Ca <1.9 or tetany/seizures):
→ Calcium gluconate 10% 20ml (2.2mmol Ca) IV over 10-20 min, then infusion
→ Calcium chloride 10% 10ml IV (more irritant — use for cardiac arrest / central line)
Asymptomatic: oral supplementation — Adcal-D3 / Calcichew
Replace Mg if low.

🚨 ALWAYS give thiamine BEFORE glucose in any patient with alcohol misuse or malnutrition. Glucose precipitates Wernicke's encephalopathy.
1

Wernicke's Encephalopathy — Thiamine (Pabrinex)

  • Pabrinex IV High Potency: 2 pairs (4 ampoules = 500mg thiamine) IV in 100ml NaCl over 30 min TDS × 3 days
  • Then Pabrinex 1 pair (250mg) IV OD × 5 days
  • Then oral thiamine 100mg TDS maintenance
  • Give BEFORE any dextrose-containing fluids
2

Alcohol Withdrawal — Symptom-Triggered Benzodiazepine

  • CIWA-Ar guided: treat if score >8
  • Chlordiazepoxide PO (preferred — long-acting, less addiction potential):
    CIWA 8-15: 25-50mg q2-4h prn | CIWA >15: 50-100mg q1-2h prn
    Typical reducing regime: 30mg QDS day 1 → taper over 5-7 days
  • Hepatic failure: Lorazepam 1-2mg PO/IV (safer than chlordiazepoxide as no active metabolites)
  • IV route if unable to take PO or severe withdrawal
3

Delirium Tremens (CIWA >20)

  • ICU/HDU — high mortality if untreated (5-15%)
  • Diazepam 10mg IV q5-10 min until calm (symptom-controlled — some patients need 100mg+)
  • Or Lorazepam 2-4mg IV q15 min
  • IV thiamine, IV fluids, electrolyte replacement (K, Mg, PO4)
  • Haloperidol for refractory hallucinations (adjunct only — not primary treatment)
4

Alcohol Withdrawal Seizures

  • Lorazepam 2-4mg IV — first-line (benzodiazepine, also treats withdrawal)
  • Adequate benzodiazepine dosing prevents further seizures
  • Phenytoin NOT recommended (ineffective for alcohol withdrawal seizures)
  • Ensure adequate thiamine replacement

📚 Key Guidelines & References

↗ NICE CG100 — Alcohol-Use Disorders: Diagnosis and Management of Alcohol-Related Physical Complications ↗ CIWA-Ar Scale — Sullivan et al., British Journal of Addiction 1989 ↗ NICE CKS — Wernicke's Encephalopathy

Thyroid Emergencies

RARE BUT DANGEROUS
📋 History Proforma
💊 Management

📋 History Template

THYROID EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT
==============================
Presentation: thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) / myxoedema coma

THYROID STORM FEATURES (Burch-Wartofsky Score — treat if >45):
Temp:        37.2-37.7=5 / 37.8-38.2=10 / 38.3-38.8=15 / 38.9-39.4=20 / 39.4-39.9=25 / ≥40=30: ___
CNS:         absent=0 / mild agitation=10 / moderate delirium=20 / severe seizure/coma=30: ___
GI/hepatic:  absent=0 / moderate N&V/diarrhoea=10 / jaundice=20: ___
HR:          <90=0 / 90-109=5 / 110-119=10 / 120-129=15 / 130-139=20 / ≥140=25: ___
CCF:         absent=0 / mild oedema=5 / bibasal creps=10 / pulm oedema=15: ___
AF:          absent=0 / present=10: ___
Precipitant: absent=0 / present=10: ___
BWS Total: ___  [<25 unlikely / 25-44 impending / ≥45 thyroid storm]

SYMPTOMS (THYROID STORM — hyperthyroid emergency):
□ Hyperthermia (>38.5°C)   □ Marked tachycardia / AF
□ Agitation / psychosis / confusion / seizures / coma
□ Severe diaphoresis   □ Vomiting / diarrhoea
□ CCF / high-output cardiac failure

SYMPTOMS (MYXOEDEMA COMA — hypothyroid emergency):
□ Reduced GCS / coma   □ Hypothermia (may be profound)
□ Bradycardia / hypotension   □ Hypoventilation / hypercapnia
□ Periorbital oedema / macroglossia   □ Delayed relaxation of reflexes
□ Hyponatraemia / hypoglycaemia / hypoventilation

PMHx: known thyroid disease / Graves' / previous thyroidectomy / RAI
Medications: propylthiouracil / carbimazole / levothyroxine — compliance: Y/N
PRECIPITANT (storm):
□ Infection   □ Surgery/trauma   □ Iodine contrast   □ MI   □ Non-compliance with antithyroid drugs
□ Parturition   □ Amiodarone

EXAMINATION:
Temp: ___   HR: ___   BP: ___/___   RR: ___   SpO2: ___%   GCS: ___/15
Skin: warm+moist (storm) / dry+cold (myxoedema)   Goitre: Y/N
Eyes: exophthalmos / lid lag (Graves')
Thyroid storm: tremor / tachycardia / fever / flushed / agitated
Myxoedema: hypothermic / bradycardic / dry skin / non-pitting oedema / slow speech

INVESTIGATIONS:
TSH: ___   Free T4: ___   Free T3: ___
FBC / U&E / LFTs / glucose / cortisol (Addison's coexistence)
ECG (AF / heart block / bradycardia)   CXR   Blood cultures (if infection trigger)

IMPRESSION:
□ Thyroid storm (BWS ___) — treat empirically if ≥45
□ Impending storm (BWS 25-44) — treat
□ Myxoedema coma — treat empirically
1

Thyroid Storm — Treatment Sequence

  • Step 1 — Block synthesis: Propylthiouracil (PTU) 500-1000mg PO/NG stat, then 250mg 4-hourly (preferred over carbimazole in storm — also blocks T4→T3 conversion)
  • Step 2 — Block release (1h AFTER PTU): Lugol's iodine 5-10 drops PO TDS or potassium iodide (give 1h after thionamide to prevent iodine fuelling synthesis)
  • Step 3 — Block peripheral effects: Propranolol 60-80mg PO q4-6h (or IV if unable to take PO) — controls tachycardia, tremor, anxiety. Use esmolol infusion if CCF.
  • Step 4 — Block T4→T3: Hydrocortisone 100mg IV TDS (covers relative adrenal insufficiency + inhibits conversion)
  • Treat precipitant: antibiotics, cooling, IVF
  • ICU admission. Endocrinology referral urgently.
2

Myxoedema Coma

  • Airway protection — intubate if GCS declining, hypoventilating
  • IV Levothyroxine (T4) 300-500mcg IV bolus then 50-100mcg OD IV (discuss dose with endocrinology)
  • Plus T3 (liothyronine) 5-20mcg IV if available — faster onset
  • Hydrocortisone 100mg IV TDS — always give before thyroid hormone (exclude/treat relative Addison's)
  • Passive rewarming — avoid active external rewarming (causes peripheral vasodilation + shock)
  • Correct hyponatraemia slowly. Treat hypoglycaemia. IV fluids cautiously (risk CCF).
  • ICU. Endocrinology referral urgently.
