ENT Emergencies

TIME-SENSITIVE
📋 History Proforma
💊 Management

📋 History Template

ENT EMERGENCY ASSESSMENT
=========================
Presentation: □ Epistaxis  □ Stridor / airway threat  □ Quinsy / peritonsillar abscess
              □ Epiglottitis  □ Foreign body  □ Mastoiditis  □ Acute otitis media

STRIDOR / UPPER AIRWAY ASSESSMENT:
⚠️ If stridor present: senior airway help immediately — anaesthetics + ENT
Stridor: Y/N   Type: inspiratory (laryngeal) / expiratory (tracheal) / biphasic (severe)
Voice: normal / hoarse / muffled (hot potato voice = quinsy/epiglottitis)
Drooling: Y/N   Dysphagia: Y/N   Tripod posture: Y/N
SpO2: ___%   Stridor at rest: Y/N

EPIGLOTTITIS (do NOT examine throat with tongue depressor without airway support):
□ Rapid onset sore throat + dysphagia + fever   □ Drooling   □ Tripod posture
□ Muffled/hot potato voice   □ Unable to swallow
□ Unvaccinated / immunocompromised
→ Senior airway support first. Soft-tissue lateral neck XR (thumb sign) or CT.
→ Do NOT attempt intubation without ENT/anaesthetics present.

QUINSY / PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS:
□ Unilateral severe throat pain   □ Trismus (mouth opening: ___ cm)
□ Uvular deviation to contralateral side   □ Unilateral peritonsillar swelling
□ Hot potato voice   □ Drooling   □ Fever

EPISTAXIS:
Side: L / R / bilateral   Anterior / posterior (blood into pharynx)
Amount: minor / moderate / major (>500ml / haemodynamically compromising)
Duration: ___   Active at time of assessment: Y/N
Previous episodes: Y/N   Previous cautery/packing: Y/N
Anticoagulants / antiplatelets: Y/N — which: ___   Last dose: ___
Liver disease / haematological disorder: Y/N
BP: ___/___ (hypertension is a risk factor)
Examine: Little's area (anterior septum — commonest site)

PMHx: bleeding disorder / coagulopathy / hypertension / URTI
Medications: warfarin / DOACs / aspirin / clopidogrel / NSAIDs

EXAMINATION:
HR: ___  BP: ___/___  SpO2: ___%
Throat: erythema / exudate / swelling / uvular deviation / peritonsillar bulge
Tonsils: size 1-4+ / unilateral enlargement
Neck: cervical lymphadenopathy / stiffness / swelling
Ear: TM appearance (AOM / effusion) / mastoid tenderness
Posterior rhinoscopy / anterior rhinoscopy (Thudichum speculum): ___

IMPRESSION:
□ Epiglottitis — AIRWAY EMERGENCY
□ Quinsy — ENT for aspiration/incision
□ Ludwig's angina — floor of mouth cellulitis — AIRWAY EMERGENCY
□ Retropharyngeal abscess — CT neck + ENT
□ Epistaxis — anterior / posterior / severe
🚨 Any stridor + inability to manage secretions = Airway Emergency — call anaesthetics + ENT simultaneously. Do not leave patient alone.
1

Epiglottitis

  • Sit patient upright. Do NOT lay down. Do NOT examine throat without airway team present.
  • Humidified O₂. Alert anaesthetics + ENT immediately.
  • IV access (calmly — anxiety worsens obstruction). Dexamethasone 8mg IV.
  • Ceftriaxone 2g IV (covers H. influenzae and Streptococcal)
  • Definitive airway (intubation or surgical) in controlled setting — theatre if possible
2

Quinsy (Peritonsillar Abscess)

  • ENT referral for aspiration or incision & drainage
  • Benzylpenicillin 1.2g IV QDS + Metronidazole 500mg IV TDS
  • Dexamethasone 8-10mg IV (reduces oedema and pain)
  • Adequate analgesia. IV fluids if unable to swallow.
  • Quinsy tonsillectomy: 6 weeks after resolution
3

Epistaxis

  • First aid: lean forward, pinch soft part of nose (not bridge) continuously for 15-20 min, mouth breathe
  • Examine: good light + Thudichum speculum after suction to identify bleeding point
  • Anterior bleed (Little's area):
    Topical: Lidocaine + adrenaline spray then silver nitrate cautery (one side only per episode)
    If uncontrolled: Nasopore/Rapid Rhino anterior nasal pack
  • Posterior bleed / anterior pack fails:
    ENT referral. Posterior balloon pack (Foley catheter 12-14Fr). Consider surgery/embolisation.
  • Anticoagulation: reverse only if life-threatening — discuss with haematology
  • Discharge: saline nasal spray, avoid nose blowing, no strenuous activity 2 weeks. Return if rebleeds.
4

Ludwig's Angina (Floor-of-mouth cellulitis)

  • Airway emergency — senior anaesthetics + ENT immediately
  • Co-amoxiclav 1.2g IV TDS + Metronidazole 500mg IV TDS
  • Early surgical drainage. ICU. Awake fibreoptic intubation if airway compromised.
5

Acute Mastoiditis

  • CT temporal bones (confirms diagnosis, identifies complications)
  • Ceftriaxone 2g IV BD — empirical
  • ENT urgently — may need myringotomy ± cortical mastoidectomy
  • Complications: subperiosteal abscess, meningitis, sinus thrombosis — CT head also

Autonomic Nervous System — Sympathetic & Parasympathetic

Pharmacology Reference
🧭 Overview
⚡ Sympathetic / Adrenergic
🌿 Parasympathetic / Cholinergic
🗺️ Organ Effects Map
🚨 EM Clinical Correlations

Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic — Quick Comparison

FeatureSympatheticParasympathetic
OriginThoracolumbar (T1–L2)Craniosacral (CN III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4)
Ganglia locationClose to spinal cord (paravertebral chain / prevertebral)Close to or within the target organ
Preganglionic fibreShortLong
Postganglionic fibreLongShort
Preganglionic transmitterAcetylcholine → nicotinic (Nn)Acetylcholine → nicotinic (Nn)
Postganglionic transmitterNoradrenaline (except sweat glands = ACh/muscarinic)Acetylcholine → muscarinic
Adrenal medullaDirectly innervated by preganglionic fibres — releases adrenaline (~80%) + noradrenaline (~20%) straight into blood (a "modified ganglion")Not applicable
Overall role"Fight or flight" — mobilises energy, ↑HR/BP, bronchodilation, mydriasis, shunts blood to muscle"Rest and digest" — conserves energy, ↓HR, stimulates digestion/secretions, miosis
⚠️ Exception to remember: sweat glands are innervated by sympathetic postganglionic fibres, but the neurotransmitter is acetylcholine acting on muscarinic (M3) receptors — not noradrenaline. This is a classic exam trap.

Parasympathetic Cranial Nerve Outflow ("Rule of 3, 7, 9, 10")

CN III (Oculomotor): Edinger-Westphal nucleus → ciliary ganglion → pupil constriction (sphincter pupillae) + accommodation (ciliary muscle)
CN VII (Facial): → pterygopalatine/submandibular ganglia → lacrimal gland, submandibular + sublingual salivary glands
CN IX (Glossopharyngeal): → otic ganglion → parotid gland
CN X (Vagus): → terminal ganglia in/near organ walls → heart, lungs, GI tract to splenic flexure (~75% of all parasympathetic outflow)
S2–S4 (Pelvic splanchnic nerves): → descending colon, rectum, bladder, genitalia

Adrenergic Receptors

ReceptorG-ProteinKey LocationsEffect of Stimulation
α1Gq (↑IP3/Ca²⁺)Vascular smooth muscle (skin/splanchnic/mucosa), iris radial muscle, GI/bladder sphincters, liverVasoconstriction (↑BP), mydriasis, sphincter contraction, glycogenolysis, ejaculation
α2Gi (↓cAMP)Presynaptic nerve terminals, CNS, pancreatic β-cellsInhibits further NA release (negative feedback), CNS sedation/analgesia, inhibits insulin release
β1Gs (↑cAMP)Heart (SA node, myocardium), kidney (JG cells)↑HR (chronotropy), ↑contractility (inotropy), ↑conduction velocity, renin release
β2Gs (↑cAMP)Bronchial smooth muscle, skeletal muscle vasculature, uterus, liverBronchodilation, vasodilation, uterine relaxation, glycogenolysis, K⁺ shift into cells, tremor
β3Gs (↑cAMP)Adipose tissue, bladder detrusorLipolysis, detrusor relaxation (bladder storage)

💊 Drugs Acting on Adrenergic Receptors (EM-relevant)

Agonists

  • Adrenaline — α1/α2/β1/β2, dose-dependent (anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, refractory shock)
  • Noradrenaline — mainly α1, some β1 (septic shock vasopressor)
  • Dobutamine — mainly β1 (cardiogenic shock inotrope)
  • Salbutamol — β2 selective (asthma/COPD, hyperkalaemia)
  • Phenylephrine — pure α1 (vasopressor, mydriatic)
  • Clonidine — α2 agonist (antihypertensive, sedation, opioid/alcohol withdrawal)

Antagonists

  • Propranolol — non-selective β-blocker
  • Bisoprolol / Metoprolol — β1-selective
  • Doxazosin / Prazosin — α1 antagonist (hypertension, phaeochromocytoma prep)
  • Phentolamine — α blocker (cocaine-associated chest pain, extravasation)

Nicotinic Receptors (ionotropic — ligand-gated Na⁺/K⁺ channels, fast)

SubtypeLocationEffect
Nn (neuronal)All autonomic ganglia (sympathetic AND parasympathetic), adrenal medullaFast excitatory ganglionic transmission — mediates ALL preganglionic → postganglionic signalling
Nm (muscle)Neuromuscular junction (skeletal muscle)Skeletal muscle contraction (not part of the autonomic outflow itself, but same receptor family)

Muscarinic Receptors (metabotropic — GPCRs, slow)

ReceptorG-ProteinKey LocationsEffect of Stimulation
M1GqCNS, gastric parietal cellsMemory/cognition, ↑gastric acid secretion
M2GiHeart (SA/AV node)↓HR (bradycardia), ↓AV conduction velocity
M3GqSmooth muscle (bronchi, GI, bladder detrusor, iris sphincter/ciliary muscle), exocrine glands (salivary, lacrimal, sweat)Bronchoconstriction, ↑GI motility/secretions, bladder contraction, miosis + accommodation, secretions
M4GiCNS (basal ganglia)Modulates dopamine release
M5GqCNS (substantia nigra), some vasculatureMinor clinical relevance

💊 Drugs Acting on Cholinergic Receptors (EM-relevant)

Muscarinic Antagonists

  • Atropine — non-selective (bradycardia, organophosphate poisoning, antisialagogue)
  • Glycopyrronium — peripheral only, doesn't cross BBB (drying secretions, RSI, avoids reflex bradycardia)
  • Ipratropium / Tiotropium — inhaled M3 antagonist (asthma/COPD bronchodilation)
  • Hyoscine butylbromide — peripheral antispasmodic (GI/renal colic)
  • Hyoscine hydrobromide — crosses BBB, sedating (excess secretions, motion sickness)

Cholinesterase Inhibitors (↑ACh)

  • Neostigmine — reverses non-depolarising NMJ blockade; myasthenia gravis (give with glycopyrronium to blunt muscarinic bradycardia/secretions)
  • Pyridostigmine — long-term myasthenia gravis management
  • Organophosphates — irreversible AChE inhibition → cholinergic toxidrome (see Clinical Correlations tab)

🗺️ Organ-by-Organ Effects Map

Organ / SystemSympathetic EffectParasympathetic Effect
Heart↑HR, ↑contractility, ↑conduction (β1)↓HR, ↓AV conduction (M2); minimal effect on ventricular contractility
LungsBronchodilation, ↓secretions (β2)Bronchoconstriction, ↑secretions (M3)
EyesMydriasis (α1, radial muscle); far visionMiosis, accommodation for near vision (M3)
GI tract↓motility, ↓secretions, sphincter contraction↑motility, ↑secretions, sphincter relaxation
BladderDetrusor relaxation (β3), internal sphincter contraction (α1) — storageDetrusor contraction, sphincter relaxation (M3) — voiding
Salivary glandsThick, viscous secretion (α1)Copious, watery secretion (M3)
Sweat glands↑Sweating — sympathetic pathway, but cholinergic/M3 receptor (exception!)Not innervated
LiverGlycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis (α1/β2)Minimal effect
Blood vessels (skin/splanchnic)Vasoconstriction (α1)Minimal direct innervation
Blood vessels (skeletal muscle)Vasodilation (β2)Minimal
GenitaliaEjaculation (α1) — "Shoot"Erection (M3, vasodilation) — "Point"
Adrenal medullaDirect preganglionic innervation → catecholamine releaseNot applicable
💡 Mnemonic: "Point and Shoot" — Parasympathetic = Point (erection), Sympathetic = Shoot (ejaculation).
1

Anaphylaxis — why adrenaline is first-line

Adrenaline IM works via all three key receptors simultaneously: α1 — vasoconstriction, reverses hypotension and mucosal oedema; β1 — ↑HR and contractility; β2 — bronchodilation and stabilises mast cells, reducing further mediator release. No other drug (antihistamine, steroid) acts on airway/circulation this fast — see the Anaphylaxis page for the full protocol.

2

Cholinergic Toxidrome — Organophosphate / Nerve Agent Poisoning

Muscarinic effects (SLUDGE / DUMBELS): Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis / Diaphoresis, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia + Bronchorrhoea + Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation.
Nicotinic effects: muscle fasciculations, weakness progressing to paralysis, tachycardia and hypertension (can mask/oppose the muscarinic bradycardia).
Management: decontaminate first (protect yourself), Atropine 2mg IV, doubling every 3–5 min until secretions dry (titrate to secretions, NOT heart rate), Pralidoxime if available and given early (reactivates AChE before "ageing"), anticipate prolonged ventilatory support. Discuss with TOXBASE/NPIS.

3

Anticholinergic Toxidrome

Causes: TCA overdose, antihistamines, hyoscine/atropine excess, some plants (deadly nightshade).
Mnemonic: "Mad as a hatter" (agitation/delirium), "blind as a bat" (mydriasis, blurred vision), "red as a beet" (flushed skin), "hot as a hare" (hyperthermia), "dry as a bone" (dry skin/mucosae, urinary retention), "full as a flask" (urinary retention, ileus).
Management: supportive, Benzodiazepines for agitation/seizures, active cooling if hyperthermic. Physostigmine is rarely used and specialist-guided only (risk of seizures/asystole, especially in TCA overdose).

4

Sympathomimetic Toxidrome

Causes: cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA. Features: tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis, diaphoresis, agitation.
Management: Benzodiazepines first-line. Avoid unopposed beta-blockade in cocaine toxicity — blocking β2 vasodilation while α1 vasoconstriction continues unopposed risks worsening coronary vasospasm/hypertension. Use Phentolamine or benzodiazepines instead if vasospasm/chest pain.

5

Beta-Blocker vs Calcium Channel Blocker Overdose

Both cause bradycardia + hypotension. BB overdose → hypoglycaemia (blocked glycogenolysis); CCB overdose → hyperglycaemia (blocked insulin release from pancreatic Ca²⁺ channels) — a useful bedside discriminator.
Management: Atropine, Glucagon 5-10mg IV (bypasses the β-receptor, directly activates cardiac cAMP — specific for BB overdose), High-dose insulin-euglycaemia therapy, Calcium chloride/gluconate (especially CCB), IV lipid emulsion for refractory cases. Discuss early with TOXBASE/cardiology/ITU.

6

Neuromuscular Blockade (Nm receptor)

Suxamethonium — depolarising Nm agonist (RSI). Rocuronium / Vecuronium — non-depolarising Nm antagonists. Reversal: Sugammadex (rocuronium/vecuronium-specific) or Neostigmine + Glycopyrronium (glycopyrronium blunts the muscarinic bradycardia/secretions that neostigmine would otherwise cause).

7

Peri-Arrest Bradycardia

Atropine 500mcg IV (M2 antagonist) is first-line per RCUK peri-arrest bradycardia algorithm, repeated to max 3mg, before transcutaneous pacing or second-line agents (isoprenaline/adrenaline infusion).

📚 Key References

↗ BNF — British National Formulary ↗ RCUK — 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines (Peri-Arrest Bradycardia Algorithm) ↗ TOXBASE — Organophosphate / Anticholinergic / Sympathomimetic Toxidromes ↗ NPIS — National Poisons Information Service: 0344 892 0111

RCUK 2025 Resuscitation Guidelines — Algorithms

ResuscitationPublished Oct 2025
🫀 Adult ALS
📉 Peri-Arrest Arrhythmias
🧒 Paediatric BLS/PALS
👶 Newborn (NLS)
🌡️ Post-ROSC Care
⚠️ Special Circumstances
ℹ️ 2025 vs 2021: No major changes to the core adult ALS algorithm. Refinements: pad placement emphasis (lateral pad below the armpit, mid-axillary line), greater emphasis on effective ventilation, adrenaline timing unchanged, refractory VF now favours a vector-change pad position, and dual sequential defibrillation is NOT recommended by RCUK.

Non-Shockable Rhythm (PEA / Asystole)

1

CPR 30:2 (or continuous compressions once airway secured) — identify PEA/asystole.

2

Give Adrenaline 1mg IV/IO as soon as possible, then every 3–5 min.

3

CPR 2-min cycles; reassess rhythm/pulse at each pause. Identify and treat reversible causes (4H4T).

Shockable Rhythm (VF / pVT)

1

Give 1 shock as soon as identified (any VF amplitude) — minimise pre/post-shock pause to <5s. Resume CPR immediately for 2 min.

2

If shockable rhythm persists: 2nd shock, resume CPR 2 min.

3

3rd shock → immediately after: Adrenaline 1mg IV/IO + Amiodarone 300mg IV/IO (or lidocaine 100mg if amiodarone unavailable).

4

4th shock, CPR 2 min, reassess.

5

5th shock → Adrenaline 1mg IV/IO + Amiodarone 150mg IV/IO (2nd dose). Continue adrenaline every 3–5 min thereafter (alternate 2-min cycles).

⚡ Defibrillation Energy

  • Biphasic first shock: ≥150J (pulsed biphasic 130–150J)
  • If unsure of device settings, use maximum energy for all shocks
  • Reasonable to escalate energy for subsequent shocks if device allows
  • Refractory VF (persists after 3 shocks): consider vector-change — fresh pads in antero-posterior position
  • Dual sequential defibrillation — not recommended (RCUK)

💨 Airway/Ventilation

  • Highest feasible FiO2 during CPR
  • Once tracheal tube/SGA in situ: ventilate 10/min, continuous compressions (30:2 if SGA leaking)
  • Tidal volume 6–8 mL/kg IBW if mechanically ventilated
  • Waveform capnography mandatory to confirm tube placement
  • Video laryngoscopy preferred where available

Reversible Causes — 4H & 4T

4HTreatment4TTreatment
Hypoxia100% O2, secure airwayTension pneumothoraxNeedle/finger thoracostomy
HypovolaemiaCrystalloid/blood, control haemorrhageTamponadePericardiocentesis/thoracotomy
Hyper/hypokalaemia, metabolicCorrect electrolytes/glucoseThrombosis (PE/MI)Consider thrombolysis
HypothermiaActive rewarmingToxinsSpecific antidote if available

Vascular access: attempt IV first; if not achieved within 2 attempts, go IO. Do not routinely give calcium, sodium bicarbonate or corticosteroids.

📄 Official RCUK Poster — Adult ALS Algorithm 2025

📄 Official RCUK Poster — Adult In-Hospital Algorithm 2025

⚠️ Assess for life-threatening features in any unstable arrhythmia: Shock (SBP<90), Syncope, Heart failure, Myocardial ischaemia. Unstable + adverse signs (or immediately post-ROSC) → synchronised electrical cardioversion is first-line for tachyarrhythmia.

Tachyarrhythmia — Synchronised Cardioversion Energies

RhythmInitial ShockNotes
Atrial fibrillationMax output initial shockEscalating strategy not favoured — go straight to max
Atrial flutter / SVT70–120JStepwise increase if needed
VT with a pulse120–150JStepwise increase if first shock fails

If cardioversion fails and patient remains unstable: Amiodarone 300mg IV over 10–20 min (± 900mg/24h infusion) or procainamide 10–15mg/kg (max 1g) over 20 min, then re-attempt cardioversion.

Bradycardia Algorithm

1

Adverse signs present? → Atropine 500mcg IV, repeat every 3–5 min to a max of 3mg.

2

Atropine ineffective → second-line: Isoprenaline 5mcg/min or Adrenaline 2–10mcg/min infusion.

3

Refractory/unstable → transcutaneous pacing as bridge to transvenous pacing (establish early).

4

Beta-blocker/CCB cause → consider glucagon. High-degree AV block with wide QRS → atropine ineffective, go straight to pacing.

🚫 Cardiac transplant / spinal cord injury: do NOT give atropine (risk of high-degree AV block/sinus arrest) — use aminophylline 100–200mg slow IV instead.

📄 Official RCUK Poster — Adult Tachyarrhythmia Algorithm 2025

📄 Official RCUK Poster — Adult Bradyarrhythmia Algorithm 2025

Paediatric BLS Sequence

1

Check responsiveness (verbal/tactile, no painful stimuli) → open airway (head-tilt-chin-lift; neutral in infants).

2

Look/listen/feel for breathing ≤10s → give 5 initial rescue breaths.

3

No signs of life → start chest compressions immediately. Ratio 15:2 if trained in PBLS; 30:2 for untrained/adult-BLS-only rescuers.

4

Rate 100–120/min, depth ≥⅓ AP chest diameter (5–6cm in adolescents, never >6cm). Two-thumb encircling technique <1yr; one/two-hand >1yr.

🔋 AED Pad Placement

  • <25kg (≈<8yr): paediatric mode if available; antero-posterior pads
  • >25kg / adolescents: standard adult mode, antero-lateral (or AP) pads
  • No paediatric mode/pads available → use standard adult AED unmodified

🍽️ Choking (FBAO)

  • Coughing effective → encourage coughing
  • Ineffective → up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 chest thrusts (infant) or abdominal thrusts (child/adolescent), alternating
  • Unconscious → start CPR with 5 rescue breaths first

PALS Drug Doses & Defibrillation

Drug/ShockDoseTiming
Adrenaline IV/IO10 mcg/kg (max 1mg)ASAP (non-shockable); after 3rd shock (shockable); then every 3–5 min
Amiodarone IV/IO5 mg/kg (max 300mg), then 5mg/kg (max 150mg)After 3rd shock, repeat after 5th shock (shockable only)
Defibrillation4 J/kg (max 120–200J) initial; escalate up to 8 J/kg (max 360J) for refractory VF/pVT (>5 shocks)Each shockable rhythm check

Chest compressions should also start for bradycardia <60/min with poor perfusion despite adequate respiratory support, even with a detectable pulse. Change compressor every 2 min.

Paediatric Reversible Causes (4H4T) — Key Doses

CauseTreatment
Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.5–7 mmol/L)Insulin 0.1 unit/kg (max 10U) + glucose 5mL/kg 10% (max 250mL) IV bolus; nebulised/IV salbutamol 5mcg/kg
Severe hypokalaemia (<2.5 mmol/L)Potassium 1 mmol/kg (max 30mmol) at 2mmol/min over 10 min
HypoglycaemiaGlucose 0.2 g/kg IV (2mL/kg 10% glucose)
Hypovolaemia10 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid or blood bolus
Hypothermia <30°CSingle adrenaline dose + max 3 shocks until >30°C
Hypothermia 30–35°CAdrenaline every 8 min; 2nd amiodarone dose at 8 min; normal 2-min shock interval
ℹ️ Weight/dosing: use parent-reported weight where available; otherwise length-based method corrected for body habitus. Use ideal body weight (not actual) for hydrophilic drugs in children with high BMI to avoid toxicity.
ℹ️ Key 2025 changes: reduced emphasis on skin colour for assessment; two-person jaw thrust preferred when staff available; video laryngoscopy favoured for intubation; CPAP/PEEP standardised at 6 cmH2O; adrenaline interval simplified to every 4 min; sodium bicarbonate removed from the algorithm.

Initial Assessment & Airway

1

Assess breathing, heart rate (auscultation ± ECG/pulse oximetry preferred), tone. Dry/stimulate/wrap. Reassess every 30s.

2

Not breathing/HR<100 → open airway, neutral position, two-person jaw thrust if available.

3

Give 5 inflation breaths (2–3s each) within 60s of birth: 30 cmH2O if ≥32 weeks, 25 cmH2O if <32 weeks. Start PEEP 6 cmH2O if PPV needed.

4

No chest rise → reapply mask/reposition, try alternative airway manoeuvre, then consider increasing pressure. Consider SGA if face-mask ineffective.

5

Chest rise achieved → give ventilation breaths 30/min for 30s, reassess HR.

🎯 Initial Oxygen & SpO2 Targets

  • ≥32 weeks needing support: start 21% O2
  • <32 weeks: start ≥30% O2
  • 3 min: 70–75% · 5 min: 80–85% · 10 min: 85–95%
  • Reduce O2 if SpO2 >95%

💛 Chest Compressions

  • Start if HR <60/min after 30s of effective ventilation
  • Ratio 3:1 (90 compressions : 30 breaths/min = 120 events/min)
  • Two-thumb encircling technique, ⅓ AP diameter depth
  • Increase O2 to 100%; secure airway (SGA/ETT) with minimal interruption

Drugs (once ventilation + compressions optimised, HR persistently <60)

DrugDose/RouteNotes
Adrenaline UVC/IO20 mcg/kg (0.2mL/kg of 1:10,000)Repeat every 4 min if HR <60
Adrenaline ET (if no UVC/IO yet)100 mcg/kg (1mL/kg of 1:10,000)Give UVC/IO dose as soon as access obtained, regardless of ET timing
Glucose200 mg/kg (2mL/kg 10%)If confirmed low (~<2.6 mmol/L)
Volume10 mL/kg group O Rh-neg blood or crystalloidSuspected blood loss / unresponsive to resus
Sodium bicarbonateNo longer recommended — removed from 2025 algorithm
⚠️ Umbilical vein is preferred emergency access (clean, not sterile, technique acceptable for speed); IO is the alternative if UVC fails. Cord clamping: if intact and resuscitation needed, clamp within <30s to avoid delaying intervention; do not milk cords <28 weeks.

Immediate Post-ROSC Bundle

SystemTarget
OxygenationSpO2 94–98% — titrate FiO2, avoid hyperoxia
VentilationNormocapnia (avoid hypo-/hyperventilation)
CirculationSBP >100 mmHg or MAP 60–65 mmHg
Coronary reperfusionImmediate angiography if ST-elevation or high suspicion of coronary occlusion
TemperatureActively prevent fever — target ≤37.5°C for 24–72h if comatose. Do NOT actively rewarm mild spontaneous hypothermia (32–36°C) to normothermia
GlucoseAvoid tight glycaemic control (hypoglycaemia risk in comatose patients); treat hyperglycaemia — associated with worse neurological outcome

⚡ Seizure Management

  • Levetiracetam or sodium valproate first-line antiepileptic, plus sedatives
  • Do not give seizure prophylaxis routinely
  • Use EEG to diagnose electrographic seizures and monitor treatment response

🔮 Prognostication

  • Delay ≥72 hours in comatose/sedated patients
  • Multimodal approach — no single test used in isolation
  • Incorporate pre-arrest status, arrest context (witnessed, bystander CPR, first rhythm), and post-arrest course

Traumatic Cardiac Arrest

1

Treat as a distinct pathway — control catastrophic external haemorrhage first (tourniquet/direct pressure) before airway.

2

Bilateral finger thoracostomy (or needle decompression) for suspected tension pneumothorax; pelvic binder if suspected pelvic fracture.

3

Correct hypovolaemia (blood products), minimise crystalloid. Consider resuscitative thoracotomy if signs of life within 10–15 min of loss of output and appropriate expertise available.

🤰 Pregnancy (>20 weeks)

  • Manual left uterine displacement preferred over lateral tilt (easier to maintain quality compressions)
  • Standard pad position and defibrillation energy — do not withhold shocks
  • Perimortem caesarean section by 5 min if no ROSC (delivery aids maternal resuscitation)

💉 Hyperkalaemia (Adult)

  • Insulin-dextrose, nebulised/IV salbutamol, calcium gluconate 10% 10mL IV for cardioprotection
  • Consider extracorporeal potassium removal (dialysis) in refractory arrest

💊 Local Anaesthetic Toxicity (LAST)

  • Stop LA immediately; 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus then infusion
  • Reduce individual adrenaline doses; avoid vasopressin, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers and further local anaesthetic as an antiarrhythmic

🌊 Drowning

  • Give 5 rescue breaths first (hypoxic arrest) before compressions
  • Extended resuscitation attempts are reasonable given good outcomes reported after prolonged submersion in cold water

🫁 Pulmonary Embolism

  • Consider immediate thrombolysis if PE is the suspected/confirmed cause of arrest
  • Consider continuing CPR for 60–90 min after thrombolytic administration

🥶 Hypothermic Arrest

  • <30°C: single adrenaline dose, max 3 shocks, withhold further until >30°C (unless proceeding to ECLS)
  • 30–35°C: adrenaline every 8 min, standard 2-min shock interval
  • Prioritise transfer to a centre capable of extracorporeal rewarming
⚠️ Asthma in cardiac arrest: consider disconnecting the ventilator circuit and applying manual chest compression/decompression to relieve dynamic hyperinflation (gas trapping) before assuming PEA is due to another cause; consider bilateral thoracostomy to exclude tension pneumothorax.
